title: 布加迪推出定制超跑 Destrier：赛道机器 Bolide 变身优雅艺术品，全球仅此一台
content:
IT之家 8 月 6 日消息，布加迪把为赛道而生的 Bolide 改造成了一款截然相反的作品 ——Destrier，新车不再执着于圈速，而是把设计、情感和手工工艺放在首位。
Destrier 全球仅此一辆，不过这并不影响各位IT之家家友将其设为壁纸。其沿用了 Bolide 的极端机械基础，却走上了完全不同的道路。布加迪拆除了大量强调性能的空气动力学部件，把一台凶悍的赛道机器重新塑造成优雅的孤品超跑。
新车是 Programme Solitaire 孤品定制项目继 Brouillard 和 FKP Hommage 之后推出的第三款作品。Destrier 得名于中世纪骑士所骑乘的名贵战马，保留 Bolide 的碳纤维单体壳，车身高度却只有 1001mm，刷新了布加迪量产及定制车型的最低车身纪录。
新车完全舍弃了 Bolide 夸张的尾翼和附加空气动力学套件，整车轮廓因而显得更纯粹、更舒展。此外，布加迪还重新处理了品牌标志性的 C 形线条。腰线沿车侧延伸，在前轮拱后方短暂消失，再与更加宽阔的马蹄形格栅衔接。车头褪去了 Bolide 咄咄逼人的赛道气息，车尾则融入一道低调的整体式尾翼，灵感来自 Chiron Profilée。
布加迪设计总监弗兰克 · 海尔表示：“Destrier 不是一款需要用头脑理解的汽车，而是一款需要用心感受的汽车。”
其设计思路可以追溯到传奇的 Type 57。同一套基础既孕育了赢得勒芒冠军的 Type 57G Tank 赛车，也造就了汽车设计史上的经典 ——Type 57SC Atlantic。
Destrier 采用名为 Sapphire Celeste 的专属深蓝色车漆。漆面加入类似钻石的细微颗粒，光线变化时会呈现独特闪烁效果，再配合抛光铝饰件和带蓝色色泽的碳纤维部件，整车显得克制而华丽。
座舱则彻底摆脱 Bolide 的纯赛车风格，大幅减少了裸露碳纤维和强调竞技感的材料，并以近似高级裁缝工作室的精致氛围取而代之。
暖棕色皮革、磨砂皮革和专属 3D 针织面料构成内饰主体。针织材料中织入铜线，并排列成连续的环形图案，借鉴高级定制时装，吸收高性能运动服饰的设计语言，让整个座舱保持浑然一体的手工质感。
方向盘中心、车门把手、空调出风口和迎宾踏板均采用锤纹铝制工艺，纹理酷似中世纪骑士手工锻造的铠甲，也再次呼应 Destrier 的战马寓意。
优雅外表之下，Destrier 依然搭载 Bolide 的 8.0 升四涡轮增压 W16 发动机，最大功率达到 1177kW。

title: 放弃 x86 独占：Proxmox VE 9.2 发布并首次支持 Arm64 架构
content:
IT之家 8 月 6 日消息，开源虚拟化平台 Proxmox Virtual Environment 于当地时间 8 月 5 日宣布推出 9.2 版本并正式支持 arm64/aarch64 架构，标志着该平台首次脱离 x86-64 体系。
Arm64 版本并非社区移植项目或实验性预览版本，而是与 x86-64 版本采用相同代码基础、软件仓库、版本生命周期、配置工具以及官方文档体系的正式版本。
PVE 9.2 版本基于 Debian 13.5“Trixie”开发，默认采用 Linux 内核 7.0，搭载 QEMU 11.0、LXC 7.0 和 ZFS 2.4 等相同版本的底层核心技术。
官方首发支持的硬件平台为 NVIDIA Grace Hopper 与 NVIDIA Vera CPU 架构。该版本在开发过程中与 NVIDIA 及 Supermicro 展开了技术合作，在 NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchip 服务器系统上完成了联合验证。对其他基于 UEFI 的 ARM v9-A 或更新硬件的支持属于“尽力而为”，ARM v8-A 通常也可运行，但同样属于尽力支持范围。
需要指出的是，该版本对硬件启动方式有明确要求：主机必须通过 UEFI 启动，并通过 ACPI 描述其硬件。仅依赖设备树（Device Tree）的单板计算机，例如树莓派系列，就不在官方支持范围内。
在架构差异方面，Arm64 虚拟机需要通过 Arm 版本的 OVMF 固件（AAVMF）启动，因为该架构不支持 SeaBIOS。同时，与 x86 处理器相关的部分技术，例如 AMD 安全加密虚拟化（SEV）以及 Intel GVT-g 图形虚拟化技术，也无法使用。
此外，虚拟机只能运行在相同 CPU 架构的主机上。Arm64 虚拟机必须部署于 Arm64 节点，x86-64 虚拟机则需要运行在 x86-64 硬件环境中，在线迁移功能也只能在相同架构节点之间使用。
虽然 Proxmox 并未阻止管理员将 x86-64 和 Arm64 节点加入同一集群，但官方并不支持混合架构集群。在不同架构之间，虚拟机无法直接进行在线迁移，高可用调度也需要确保虚拟机始终运行于兼容架构节点。
对于已有 x86-64 虚拟机，用户无法直接将其迁移至 Arm64 主机后启动。Proxmox 表示，相关数据可以通过离线迁移、备份恢复或共享存储方式转移，但操作系统需要重新安装或调整配置，使其适配 Arm64 架构。
Proxmox VE for Arm64 现已发布并开源，用户可在官网下载 ISO 镜像或通过软件包仓库获取。企业级支持计划可按需申请。
值得一提的是，Proxmox VE 本身为开源软件，订阅费用主要用于获取企业级支持服务与稳定更新，价格按 CPU 插槽计算，社区版订阅起价约为每年每插槽 120 欧元（IT之家注：现汇率约合 936.4 元人民币）。

title: 特斯拉 FSD v14 取消自定义限速后风波不断：超速被警方拦停后司机辩称是“自动驾驶”
content:
8 月 6 日消息，据 Electrek 今日报道，美国科罗拉多州帕克市警方于当地时间 8 月 5 日公布了一起交通违法案例。
一辆开启 FSD 功能的特斯拉车辆在限速 45 英里 / 小时（约 72 公里 / 小时）的道路上以 64 英里 / 小时（约 103 公里 / 小时）的速度行驶，被警方发现后要求停车。驾驶员被拦截后向警方辩称是自己开启了“自动驾驶”，所以超速不关他的事。
帕克警察局公布的视频显示，驾驶员在接受询问时表示：“不是我在开车，是自动驾驶辅助在开。”该驾驶员面对警方全程坚持这一说法，并要求现场联系主管人员。
帕克警察局表示，辅助驾驶并不能替代驾驶员。“无论车辆配备 ACC 自适应巡航控制、LCC 车道居中辅助还是 FSD 完全自动驾驶功能，驾驶员仍然需要对车辆安全运行承担法律责任。”
目前，特斯拉所有量产车所配备的辅助驾驶系统均属于 L2 级。虽然特斯拉将其系统命名为“Full Self-Driving（完全自动驾驶）”，但该功能官方名称中也包含“Supervised（受监督）”，并不代表车辆可以完全脱离驾驶员独立运行。
围绕此次事件，争议焦点再次集中于特斯拉 FSD 名称与实际责任之间的差异。特斯拉目前以订阅形式提供 FSD 功能，其 CEO 马斯克过去多年曾多次强调该系统具备较高自动驾驶能力。
然而，当车主因为被马斯克误导依赖 FSD 而导致出现问题时，特斯拉又会强调 FSD 仍属于需要驾驶员监督的辅助驾驶功能，驾驶员必须时刻保持注意力并需承担全部责任。
此次超速事件还涉及 FSD 速度控制机制。报道指出，特斯拉此前曾提供允许用户调整速度偏移量的设置，驾驶员可以限制车辆超过道路限速的幅度。但在后续 FSD 版本中，该功能被取消，改为提供“Sloth（慢速）”“Chill（舒适）”“Standard（标准）”“Hurry（快速）”以及“Mad Max（狂暴）”等驾驶模式。
报道援引一名车主经历称，在新版 FSD 模式下，车辆可能在驾驶员未踩下加速踏板的情况下达到明显高于限速的速度。该车主认为，如果保留此前的速度偏移设置，用户可以通过设定上限避免类似情况。
特斯拉 AI 负责人 Ashok Elluswamy 表示，公司不会采用用户设定固定速度上限的方式，并认为这种设计方式并非最佳方案。特斯拉方面更倾向于通过提升 FSD 智能化水平解决相关问题。
围绕 FSD 超速行为，部分监管机构也已关注相关问题。报道称，瑞典方面曾建议欧盟拒绝特斯拉以“FSD”名称推广该系统，除非其解决车辆超速等相关行为。
特斯拉确认不会恢复 FSD 用户自定义最高速度功能，引发车主不满
FSD 自动驾驶超速被交警拦下开罚单，车主抱怨特斯拉亲删了一项好用功能

title: 特斯拉 Terafab 晶圆厂落地得克萨斯州，马斯克豪言“把尖端制造带回美国”
content:
感谢IT之家网友 西窗 的线索投递！
IT之家 8 月 6 日消息，当地时间 6 日（今天），SpaceX 宣布将与特斯拉首期投入 168 亿美元（IT之家注：现汇率约合 1,136.05 亿元人民币），在美国得克萨斯州格赖姆斯县建设 Terafab 先进 AI 芯片制造基地。项目由特斯拉 CEO 埃隆 · 马斯克规划，旨在满足两家公司未来快速增长的芯片需求。
SpaceX 和特斯拉预计，未来数年所需的算力将远远超过现有全球芯片供应规模，Terafab 旨在帮助两家公司缩小供需缺口。两家公司的合计算力需求预计将突破 1 太瓦，远超全球当前产能。
马斯克表示，Terafab 将覆盖从设计到制造的全部芯片生产环节。“通往最令人振奋未来的根基，正在得克萨斯州形成。我们已经在得州 Starbase 设立 SpaceX 总部，开发并发射星舰，也在巴斯特罗普建设 Starlink 工厂，为全球数百万用户生产高速互联网终端。接下来，我们将在格赖姆斯县启动一项规模空前的芯片制造计划，把逻辑芯片、存储芯片和先进封装全部集中在同一座厂区。Terafab 将把尖端制造带回美国，为得州创造数千个高薪岗位，并帮助我们大规模生产用于地面和太空的 AI 芯片。”
特斯拉今年 4 月已在得克萨斯超级工厂北园区启动一座研发晶圆厂的建设，为 Terafab 正式落地铺路。

title: 福特“性价比电动皮卡”Fathom 官宣：车内空间比丰田 RAV4 大，28350 美元起售
content:
IT之家 8 月 6 日消息，北京时间今天（6 日）晚间，福特公布了下一代电动皮卡的名称、价格和更明确的上市时间。新车定名 Fathom，预计明年晚些时候推出，起售价为 28,350 美元（IT之家注：现汇率约合 19.2 万元人民币）。
Fathom 是福特全新纯电平台“Universal EV Platform”诞生的首款车型，也将承担重振电动车业务的重任。目前，大型电动皮卡 F-150 Lightning 因缺乏盈利前景停产，福特在美国销售的纯电乘用车也只剩福特电马。
在电动时代经历第一轮受挫后，福特希望借 Fathom 重新出发。新车打破了福特长期沿用传统车型名称的习惯，背后有意传递一场深层变革。
Fathom 不会走彻底精简路线。福特还称，该车价格与平价纯电小车相当，车内空间却超过了丰田 RAV4。福特 Model e 业务总经理凯 · 哈特表示：“Fathom 不是一款把配置删得所剩无几的车型。我们保留了消费者喜爱的功能，也在他们并不在意的地方削减成本。”
新车将全系标配高分辨率中控大屏，并原生集成 Apple 地图。系统能够根据电量自动规划充电停靠点、显示附近充电站，并提供实时路况和逐向导航，同时兼容 Apple CarPlay 和 Android Auto。
所有版本也都支持福特 BlueCruise 免手持驾驶辅助系统，不过车主仍需额外付费激活。双向充电、数字钥匙和前备厢同样列为全系标配。
官方此次没有揭晓新车的电池容量、续航里程和快速充电性能。哈特透露，福特已经注意到消费者对 483 公里（300 英里）续航的需求。“我们知道部分消费者希望续航达到约 483 公里，所以会提供不同选择。不过，现阶段还不能公布具体数字。我们有信心在临近上市时，为消费者准备好合适的续航方案。”
据悉，Fathom 将采用美国本土生产的方形磷酸铁锂电芯，工厂使用宁德时代授权的电池技术。

title: 网友喊话小米推“重庆特供版”空调，单联瑜称强劲风系列就是“火炉城市特供”
content:
IT之家 8 月 6 日消息，今天（6 日）下午，小米集团大家电部总经理 @单联瑜_小米大家电 在微博发布长文提到：“有网友喊话‘小米空调可以出重庆特供版吗’，我觉得，米家空调强劲风完全可以成为火炉城市的‘特供空调’。”
IT之家获悉，自 7 月 5 日起，重庆经历了长达 28 天的连续高温，7 月 21 日以来更是连续 7 天最高气温冲破 40℃。
单联瑜表示，很多人回到家把空调调到 16℃，风是有了，房间却迟迟凉不下来。问题在于普通空调都只有一套固定的控制逻辑，碰到极端环境 + 长时间高负荷运行，容易“战斗力不足”，甚至直接罢工。
单联瑜进一步解释说，该空调的“强劲”并非简单把风开大、把温度调低，而是从底层重做了一套应对极端环境的能力。
首先，它能真正“看懂”环境：实时判断环境温度、负载状态、运行时长、空间温差等信息，并动态调整风量、压缩机频率和散热策略。
当重庆式高温把空调性能推到极限，系统还可以匹配“强劲模式”，通过超频运行充分调动系统潜力，更快压住室温。
更关键的是「冷媒动态调节」技术：高温、高负荷时，主动增加系统冷媒量，强化换热和循环；房间温度降下来后，再减少冷媒量，降低耗电和温度波动。该猛的时候猛，该稳的时候稳，控温均匀，张弛有度。
单联瑜透露，小米强劲风系列空调在今年的吐鲁番空调夏测中，接受了极端环境的 2208 小时持续大“烤”，也完成了连续 24 小时“鸽子笼”封闭机位运行挑战。

content:
8 月 6 日消息，据《商业内幕》今天（6 日）报道，英伟达正在低调组建一支新的
AI 安全与网络安全工程团队
上月底集中发布的一批招聘信息首次披露了团队的存在。英伟达计划
招聘一名杰出工程师
，出任新团队的创始技术负责人，其他岗位包括
安全研究工程师、评估工程师和高级经理
。团队将对尚未部署的 AI 智能体进行安全评估，还会开发利用 AI 自动修复软件漏洞的工具。
报道认为，此举说明英伟达在押注开放权重模型和 AI 智能体的同时，
也在把 AI 安全提升到更重要的位置
。开放权重模型会公开决定模型如何运行的训练参数，但训练数据和源代码仍可保持封闭。
英伟达在一则招聘信息中称，团队秉持一项“坚定信念”：开放权重模型、技术透明度和广泛的科学审查，
是美国维持 AI 领先地位及增强网络安全防御能力的基础

英伟达创始人兼 CEO 黄仁勋上个月首次在 X 平台发文，转发了一封呼吁美国政策制定者支持开放模型的公开信。他指出，开放模型能够提高 AI 安全性并加强网络安全。
随着 AI 从只能对话的聊天机器人转向能够读取企业敏感数据、调用工具并执行现实任务的智能体，企业能否信任 AI 系统，很可能成为决定普及速度的关键。

title: 英特尔 Diamond Rapids 至强 7 ES 处理器首次现身 SiSoftware：32 核 +240MB 缓存，18A-P 工艺已跑通
content:
8 月 6 日消息，爆料者
@momomo_us
发现，英特尔下一代至强（Xeon）7 系列处理器“Diamond Rapids”的首款工程样品已经出现在了 SiSoftware 数据库中，确认其基于增强版 18A-P 工艺打造。
曝光的这颗工程样品配备了 32 个核心、64MB 二级缓存和 240MB 的三级缓存，运行频率仅为 1.1GHz，表明这是一颗非常早期的工程样品。
该芯片运行在英特尔代号为“Johnson City”的 Oakstream 参考评估平台上。Oakstream 平台是 Diamond Rapids 的配套平台，采用庞大的 LGA 9324 插槽，支持最高 650W 的 CPU 功耗。
Diamond Rapids 是 Granite Rapids（至强 6）的继任者，定位数据中心市场。该系列旗舰型号最高可配置约 192 个性能核（P-core），支持 16 通道内存与 PCIe Gen6；采用模块化设计，将 CBB 计算芯片与 IMH I/O 及内存控制器芯片分离。
此次样品采用的 18A-P 是 18A 工艺的性能增强版本。英特尔此前表示，相较 18A，18A-P 在相同功耗下可实现约 9% 的性能提升，或在相同性能下功耗降低约 18%。该工艺延续了 GAA 晶体管与 PowerVia 背面供电技术，并新增了 Power Boost 技术，设计规则与 18A 完全兼容。
在数据中心 CPU 市场的竞争中，Diamond Rapids 将直接面对 AMD 基于 Zen 6 架构的 EPYC Venice 和 Verano 系列。后者旗舰型号最高可达 256 核心，采用台积电 2nm 工艺，计划于 2026 年第三至第四季度上市。
AMD 预计其今年在数据中心 CPU 市场的收入份额将超过 50%。Diamond Rapids 预计于 2027 年正式发布，面对 AMD 的先发优势压力不小。另据此前报道，英特尔将在 Diamond Rapids 之后的 Coral Rapids 系列中恢复超线程（SMT）支持。

title: Den CO2-Fußabdruck eines Industrieprodukts einheitlich, vergleichbar und verständlich berechnen: So geht‘s
content:
Den CO2-Fußabdruck eines Industrieprodukts einheitlich, vergleichbar und verständlich berechnen: So geht‘s
Wie lässt sich der CO₂-Fußabdruck eines Produkts standardisiert, automatisiert und unternehmensübergreifend entlang der Wertschöpfungskette ermitteln? Und wie gelingt dies in Unternehmen, die dafür nur über begrenzte (Personal-)Ressourcen verfügen? »PCF Guidance«, der neue Leitfaden der Plattform Factory-X, an dem das Fraunhofer IWU mitgearbeitet hat, beschreibt Berechnungsmethoden und enthält konkrete Berechnungsbeispiele für Fertigungsprozesse wie Fräsen, Schmieden und additive Fertigung. Es erweitert den Betrachtungsraum auf die industrielle Fertigung von Produkten, die aus mehreren Teilen oder Baugruppen bestehen (diskrete Fertigung).
Der neue Factory-X-Leitfaden »PCF Guidance« ergänzt das Rulebook der Plattform Catena-X, das auf einer höheren Abstraktionsebene und mit Schwerpunkt Automobilindustrie grundlegende Berechnungsstandards setzt.
Warum den CO2-Fußabdruck erfassen? Was ist ein PCF?
Für große Unternehmen besteht bereits bzw. entsteht die Pflicht, über Klima- und Emissionsdaten zu berichten (CSRD, Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive der Europäischen Union). Dabei müssen häufig auch Emissionen aus Produkten und Lieferketten berücksichtigt werden. Noch greift die ESPR-Verordnung (Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation), die schrittweise den Digitalen Produktpass (DPP) mit umfassenden Nachhaltigkeitsdaten einführt, für den Großteil der Fertiger nicht. Doch die künftige Regulatorik führt dazu, dass viele Kunden von ihren Zulieferern bereits heute Produkt- oder Material-CO₂-Daten anfordern.
Factory X adressiert den Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) als eine zentrale Herausforderung für die diskrete Fertigung. Für einen Produkt-PCF müssen alle Beiträge zu einem durchgängigen CO₂-Fußabdruck (von der Rohstoffgewinnung bis zum Fabriktor, »Cradle-to-Gate«) aggregiert werden. Ein PCF beschreibt die einem konkreten Produkt zuzurechnenden Treibhausgasemissionen, typischerweise in kg CO₂e (CO₂-Äquivalent). Für die diskrete Fertigung bedeutet das beispielsweise, die Beiträge des Rohmaterials (Stahl, Aluminium, Kunststoff), der Transporte und vorgelagerten Lieferantenprozesse sowie den Energieverbrauch der Fertigungsanlagen und die Hilfsstoffe zu berücksichtigen – heruntergebrochen bis auf das einzelne Bauteil.
Was der Leitfaden »PCF Guidance« leistet
Ziel der Autoren ist es, den CO₂-Fußabdruck eines Produkts standardisiert und automatisiert aus Prozess-, Energie-, Material- und Logistikdaten berechenbar und über Unternehmensgrenzen hinweg nachvollziehbar zu machen. Der Leitfaden erläutert verständlich, wie Unternehmen systematisch Emissionsdaten aus Eigenfertigung und Lieferkette erfassen, zu einem Cradle-to-Gate-PCF zusammenführen und dabei Anforderungen wie Systemgrenzen oder Cut-off-Regeln (beispielsweise Grenzwerte, Stichtage oder Ausschlusskriterien) berücksichtigen.
Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der möglichst verursachungsgerechten Zuordnung von Energie- und Materialverbräuchen zu einzelnen Produkten. Dazu werden drei detaillierte Berechnungsbeispiele für ein Frästeil, ein Schmiedeteil und eine additiv gefertigte Dämpfergabel vorgestellt, inklusive Formeln, Datenquellen und der Behandlung von Ausschuss, Verpackung und Transporten.
Darüber hinaus beschreibt das Dokument, wie Emissionen in Mehrproduktfertigungen über Prozessunterteilung (»Process Subdivision«), Systemerweiterung (»System Expansion«) oder Allokation (physisch beziehungsweise wirtschaftlich) verteilt werden können. Es empfiehlt dafür die räumliche und zeitliche Prozessaufteilung durch Submetering (Einzelerfassung) und die Nutzung von Produktionsdaten, um den Anteil von Schätzungen und Zuordnungen zu reduzieren. Zusätzlich enthält der Leitfaden konkrete Praxisbeispiele zur Allokation von Gebäudeemissionen, Stillstandszeiten und Maschinenverbräuchen.
Orientierung, Hilfestellung und Angebot zur Kooperation
Der mit Beteiligung von ESTAINIUM, Siemens, dem Fraunhofer IWU und weiteren Partnern erstellte Leitfaden »PCF Guidance« (Product Carbon Footprint Guidance) entstand auf Basis des Catena‑X PCF Rulebook V4.0. Kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen bietet er eine wichtige Orientierungshilfe; das Fraunhofer IWU unterstützt gern bei der korrekten Berechnung eines PCF.
Austauschbarkeit der Daten
Über den Factory-X-Datenraum können Lieferanten und Kunden PCF-Daten standardisiert austauschen, sodass sich CO₂-Informationen entlang der gesamten Wertschöpfungskette nachvollziehen lassen. Dies schafft die Grundlage für kommende regulatorische bzw. kundenseitige Nachhaltigkeitsanforderungen.
Factory-X betrachtet dabei insbesondere den Cradle-to-Gate-Ansatz. Perspektivisch soll der Austausch von diesen Daten auch für kleine und mittlere Unternehmen auf Basis von Catena¬-X ermöglicht werden: Unternehmen behalten stets die vollständige Kontrolle über ihre Daten (Datensouveränität). Bei stark arbeitsteiligen Herstellprozessen über Unternehmensgrenzen hinweg lässt sich ein Cradle-to-Gate-Ansatz für die Ermittlung des CO2-Fußabdrucks nur im Rahmen automatisierter Prozesse und über sichere Daten-Ökosysteme effizient umsetzen.
Kurz erklärt...
DISKRETE FERTIGUNG bezeichnet die Herstellung von Produkten, die aus mehreren Teilen oder Baugruppen bestehen und meist wieder in ihre Einzelteile zerlegt werden können. Solche Produkte sind stückweise zählbar, werden aus einzelnen Komponenten montiert oder zusammengebaut und weisen oft eine hohe Variantenvielfalt auf. Ihre Fertigung basiert auf Stücklisten und Arbeitsplänen.
FACTORY-X ist ein vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördertes Projekt, das einen offenen Datenraum für die gewerbliche Wirtschaft aufbaut. Ziel ist es, Daten zwischen Unternehmen sicher, standardisiert und souverän auszutauschen, ohne dass die beteiligten Firmen die Kontrolle über ihre Daten verlieren. Der Fokus liegt auf Anwendungsfällen wie Product Carbon Footprint (PCF), Digital Product Passport (DPP), Lieferkettentransparenz, Resilienz und Nachhaltigkeit.
CATENA-X Technisch baut Factory-X auf Konzepten aus Catena X und der Verwaltungsschale (Asset Administration Shell) auf, um Daten entlang der gesamten Wertschöpfungskette interoperabel nutzbar zu machen. Catena X ist ein offenes, kollaboratives Datenökosystem insbesondere für die Automobilindustrie.
Factory-X bzw. der Leitfaden erhalten Fördermittel des Bundesministeriums für Wirtschaft und Energie bzw. der Europäischen Union.

Wie verändern neue Radwege, Fahrradstraßen oder Verkehrsberuhigungen den Radverkehr in einer Kommune? Welche Infrastrukturmaßnahmen werden von Radfahrenden angenommen und führen dazu, dass Menschen gern mit dem Fahrrad unterwegs sind? Antworten auf diese Fragen liefert RadSim, eine neue Webplattform der Technischen Universität Dresden (TUD), die ab sofort Kommunen bei der datenbasierten Radverkehrsplanung unterstützt.
Die im Rahmen des Forschungsprojekts „Radverkehrssimulation zur Verbesserung der kommunalen Radverkehrsplanung (RadSim)“ entwickelte Anwendung simuliert auf Basis wissenschaftlicher Modelle, wie sich Veränderungen im Verkehrsnetz auf die Wahl der Routen und die Verteilung der Radverkehrsströme auswirken. Kommunen können so verschiedene Szenarien simulieren, unkompliziert miteinander vergleichen und deren Auswirkungen auf den Radverkehr virtuell erproben, bevor sie umgesetzt werden. Dadurch lassen sich Planungsprozesse fundierter gestalten und Investitionsentscheidungen auf eine belastbare Datengrundlage stützen.
„Mit RadSim stellen wir erstmals ein wissenschaftliches Werkzeug bereit, mit dem sich unterschiedliche Planungsvarianten bereits vor ihrer Umsetzung realitätsnah simulieren lassen. Das schafft eine fundierte Entscheidungsgrundlage und hilft dabei, öffentliche Mittel dort einzusetzen, wo sie den größten Nutzen für den Radverkehr und die Menschen vor Ort haben“, so Projektleiter Dr.-Ing. Stefan Huber.
Wissenschaftliche Modelle auf Basis realer Routendaten
Grundlage der Simulationen sind wissenschaftlich entwickelte Modelle des Routenwahlverhaltens von Radfahrenden. Diese wurden an der Professur für Verkehrsökologie aus anonymisierten Bewegungsdaten der STADTRADELN-App entwickelt und in die Webanwendung integriert.
Die Modelle ermöglichen unter anderem Aussagen darüber, welche Maßnahmen besonders attraktiv für Radfahrende sind, wie sich Radverkehrsströme innerhalb einer Kommune durch Maßnahmen verlagern, welche Netzabschnitte stärker oder weniger genutzt werden und wie unterschiedliche Planungsvarianten im direkten Vergleich wirken.
Mehr Lebensqualität durch bessere Radverkehrsplanung
Von den Erkenntnissen profitieren nicht nur kommunale Planungsämter. Eine zielgerichtete Radverkehrsplanung schafft langfristig sicherere, komfortablere und besser vernetzte Radverkehrsangebote. Das kann mehr Menschen motivieren, Alltagswege mit dem Fahrrad zurückzulegen und trägt gleichzeitig zu weniger Verkehrslärm, geringeren Emissionen und einer höheren Aufenthaltsqualität im öffentlichen Raum bei.
Mit RadSim stellt die TUD Kommunen damit ein wissenschaftlich fundiertes Werkzeug zur Verfügung, das datenbasierte Entscheidungen erleichtert und einen wichtigen Beitrag zu einer nachhaltigen und zukunftsfähigen Mobilitätsplanung leistet.
Das Forschungsprojekt „Radverkehrssimulation zur Verbesserung der kommunalen Radverkehrsplanung (RadSim)" wird vom Bundesministerium für Verkehr (BMV) aus Mitteln zur Umsetzung des Nationalen Radverkehrsplans gefördert. Das Gesamtvolumen beträgt 621.456,74 Euro.
Die Plattform steht teilnehmenden Kommunen der Kampagne STADTRADELN mit einer ausreichenden Datengrundlage kostenfrei zur Verfügung.

Viele kleine und mittlere Unternehmen möchten Künstliche Intelligenz, Extended Reality, Automatisierung oder andere digitale Technologien nutzen. Im Tagesgeschäft fehlen jedoch oft Zeit, Ressourcen und Orientierung, um die richtigen Technologien auszuwählen und sie sinnvoll und wirtschaftlich einzusetzen.
Hier setzt das neue Projekt techHAUS des Fraunhofer FIT an: Als gefördertes Strukturwandelprojekt im Rheinischen Revier hat techHAUS den Auftrag, digitale Technologien für Unternehmen einfach zugänglich zu machen. Es entsteht ein Ort, an dem Unternehmen Zukunftstechnologien kennenlernen, ausprobieren und ihre Potenziale für das eigene Unternehmen bewerten können. Ziel ist es, Digitalisierung greifbar zu machen, Fehlinvestitionen zu vermeiden und Unternehmen dabei zu unterstützen, Innovationen schneller in die Praxis zu bringen. Dafür bündelt techHAUS die langjährige Forschungskompetenz des Fraunhofer FIT und vermittelt praxisnah den Einsatz digitaler Technologien, darunter Web3, Extended Reality und KI.
Prof. Wolfgang Prinz, Co-Projektleiter von techHAUS und stellvertretender Leiter des Fraunhofer-Instituts für Angewandte Informationstechnik FIT, bringt das Leistungsportfolio für Unternehmen auf den Punkt: »Viele Unternehmen stehen nicht vor der Frage, ob sie digitalisieren müssen, sondern wie. Genau dabei unterstützen wir. Wir helfen Unternehmen dabei, die richtigen Technologien für ihre individuellen Herausforderungen zu finden, sie praktisch auszuprobieren und fundierte Entscheidungen für ihre nächsten Digitalisierungsschritte zu treffen.«
Das Angebot richtet sich in erster Linie an kleine und mittlere Unternehmen aller Branchen. Darüber hinaus steht techHAUS auch Kommunen, Initiativen sowie Bürgerinnen und Bürgern als Anlaufstelle für Fragen rund um digitale Technologien offen. Unternehmen bringen ihre Fragestellungen und Herausforderungen ein und erhalten Orientierung bei der Bewertung digitaler Technologien sowie Impulse für ihre eigenen Digitalisierungsvorhaben. Die daraus entstehenden Demonstratoren, Methoden und Prototypen werden öffentlich zugänglich gemacht und fördern den Wissenstransfer für Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. Ergänzt wird das Angebot durch Weiterbildungen, Studien und Veranstaltungen, die Unternehmen dabei unterstützen, digitale Entwicklungen einzuordnen und gezielt für die eigene Zukunft zu nutzen.
Mit dem Projekt leistet techHAUS einen Beitrag zum Strukturwandel im Rheinischen Revier und stärkt die Innovationskraft der regionalen Wirtschaft. Das Projekt wird im Rahmen des STARK-Programms durch das Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördert und vom Ministerium für Wirtschaft, Industrie, Klimaschutz und Energie des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen begleitet.
Co-Projektleiterin Lisa Klug äußert sich folgendermaßen zur Rolle von techHAUS in der digitalen Transformation: »Digitalisierung darf keine zusätzliche Belastung sein. Sie muss Unternehmen dabei helfen, effizienter zu arbeiten, Fachkräfte zu entlasten und wettbewerbsfähig zu bleiben. Unser Ziel ist es, digitale Technologien verständlich, praxisnah und einfach zugänglich zu machen, damit aus Innovation konkrete Wertschöpfung entsteht.«
Interessierte Unternehmen können sich ab sofort unverbindlich über Workshops, Demonstrationen und Mitwirkungsmöglichkeiten im techHAUS informieren. Sie möchten mehr über das techHAUS und seine Angebote erfahren? Unsere Ansprechpartnerinnen und Ansprechpartner stehen Ihnen gerne zur Verfügung.
Die offizielle Eröffnung des techHAUS findet am 8. Oktober 2026 im Beisein von Mona Neubaur, Ministerin für Wirtschaft, Industrie, Klimaschutz und Energie des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen, statt. title: Sind Gasturbinen bereit für die Wasserstoffwirtschaft?
content:
Sind Gasturbinen bereit für die Wasserstoffwirtschaft?

Xizhen Dong untersuchte wie sich Wasserstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen auf Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen auswirkt. Solche Legierungen werden unter anderem für Turbinenschaufeln in Gasturbinen und Flugzeugen eingesetzt.
| Copyright:
Max-Planck-Institut für Nachhaltige Materialien GmbH
Download
Internationales Forschungsteam zeigt, wie Wasserstoff Turbinenwerkstoffe bei hohen Temperaturen schädigt.
Auf den Punkt gebracht:
• Herausforderung: Gasturbinen für die Stromerzeugung und Luftfahrt werden bislang mit fossilen Brennstoffen betrieben und verursachen 15% der weltweiten Kohlendioxid-Emissionen. Wasserstoff gilt als CO2-freie Alternative. Bislang war unklar, wie sich Wasserstoff bei hohen Temperaturen auf die Turbinenschaufeln aus Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen auswirkt.
• Forschungsfrage: Was geschieht mit Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen, wenn sie bei hohen Temperaturen Wasserstoff ausgesetzt werden?
• Ergebnisse: Wasserstoff versprödet den Turbinenwerkstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen mindestens doppelt so schnell wie bei Raumtemperatur. Verursacht wird die Versprödung durch chemische Reaktionen zwischen Wasserstoff und Kohlenstoff, die Karbide abbauen und Methan bilden. Dies führt zu frühem Materialversagen.
• Ausblick: Karbide erhöhen die Festigkeit von Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen. Gleichzeitig greift der Wasserstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen genau dort an. Um Gasturbinen mit Wasserstoff zu betreiben, müssen künftige Legierungen auf andere Festigungsmechanismen zurückgreifen.
Gasturbinen, die mit fossilen Brennstoffen betrieben werden, liefern 22% des globalen Stroms. Gleichzeitig sind sie für 15% der weltweiten CO2-Emissionen verantwortlich. Um Gasturbinen CO2-frei zu betreiben, könnte Wasserstoff als umweltfreundliche Alternative in Gasturbinen zur Stromerzeugung und in der Luftfahrt eingesetzt werden. Doch wie beeinflusst Wasserstoff Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen – der Werkstoff aus dem die Turbinenschaufeln bestehen – unter den extremen Bedingungen innerhalb der Turbine?
Während die Wirkung von Wasserstoff auf metallische Werkstoffe bei Raumtemperatur bereits intensiv untersucht wurde, ist über das Verhalten bei erhöhten Temperaturen wie in Gasturbinen, bislang deutlich weniger bekannt. Ein internationales Forschungsteam unter anderem vom Max-Planck-Institut für Nachhaltige Materialien (MPI-SusMat) hat untersucht, wie sich Wasserstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen auf Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen auswirkt. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die Turbinenschaufeln bei erhöhten Temperaturen mindestens doppelt so schnell verspröden wie bei Raumtemperatur. Dies stellt eine erhebliche Herausforderung für Bauteile dar, die höchsten Anforderungen an Sicherheit und Zuverlässigkeit genügen müssen.
Die Forschungsergebnisse wurden jetzt in der Fachzeitschrift Nature Materials veröffentlicht.
Warum Wasserstoff bei hohen Temperaturen schädlicher ist
„Dringt Wasserstoff bei Raumtemperatur in eine Nickelbasis-Superlegierung ein, setzt er sich in der Regel an Grenzflächen und Versetzungen fest und führt zur Versprödung. Bei erhöhten Temperaturen kommt noch ein weiterer Effekt hinzu: Wasserstoff dringt in die Karbide, die eigentlich für die Festigkeit des Werkstoffs verantwortlich sind, und verbindet sich dort mit Kohlenstoff. Wasserstoff und Kohlenstoff reagieren zu Methan, welches einen hohen lokalen Druck auf die Grenzflächen zwischen Karbiden und Nickelmatrix ausübt und so schneller zu Materialversagen führt“, erklärt Dr. Xizhen Dong, Postdoktorandin am MPI-SusMat und eine der Erstautorinnen der Studie.
Die Temperatur ist entscheidend
Dong und ihr Team untersuchten, wie sich Wasserstoff auf Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen bei Temperaturen zwischen 400°C und 1000°C auswirkt. Mithilfe der Atomsonde analysierten sie den Werkstoff auf atomarer Ebene und simulierten die Bildung von Methan mit Methoden der Dichtefunktionaltheorie. Dabei konnten sie zeigen, dass wasserstoffbedingte Schädigungen aufgrund thermodynamischer Bedingungen ausschließlich bei 400°C auftreten. Denn nur bei dieser Temperatur ist die Reaktion von Wasserstoff und Kohlenstoff zu Methan thermodynamisch begünstigt. Oberhalb von 400 °C wurde keine Methanbildung beobachtet.
„Dieses Ergebnis ist insbesondere für Gasturbinen in der Energieerzeugung und für Flugtriebwerke von großer Bedeutung“, erklärt Professor Dierk Raabe, Direktor am MPI-SusMat und einer der korrespondierenden Autoren der Studie. „Im Gegensatz zu stationären Dampfturbinen, die dauerhaft bei sehr hohen Temperaturen laufen, werden Gasturbinen häufig an- und abgeschaltet. Dadurch sind sie einem deutlich größeren Temperatur- und Belastungsspektrum ausgesetzt und genau in diesem Bereich kann wasserstoffbedingte Versprödung verstärkt auftreten.“
Zwischen hoher Festigkeit und Wasserstoffresistenz
Karbide erhöhen die Festigkeit von Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen, Stählen und Verbundwerkstoffen. Die jetzigen Untersuchungen zeigen allerdings, dass bei erhöhten Temperaturen und der Verwendung von Wasserstoff als Energieträger Karbide die Eintrittspforte für Wasserstoffversprödung sein können. Um zukünftig Gasturbinen mit Wasserstoff und somit CO2-frei betreiben zu können, sollten alternative Verfestigungsmechanismen gefunden werden. Alternativ müssten die Werkstoffe so angepasst werden, dass ein ausgewogenes Verhältnis zwischen der durch Karbide erzielten Festigkeit und der Widerstandsfähigkeit gegenüber wasserstoffinduzierter Versprödung erzielt wird.
Die Ergebnisse unterstreichen, wie wichtig es ist vorhandene Legierungen unter realen Einsatzbedingungen zu testen, um deren Sicherheit und Lebensdauer optimieren zu können.
Die Studie wurde von Forschenden der East China University of Science and Technology (China), des Max-Planck-Instituts für Nachhaltige Materialien (Deutschland) und der Hunan University (China) geleitet.

大众变速器天津公司与臻驱科技就功率模块战略合作备忘录签约
近日，大众汽车自动变速器（天津）有限公司（以下简称大众变速器天津公司）与臻驱科技（上海）股份有限公司（以下简称臻驱科技）功率模块战略合作备忘录签约仪式在天津举行。大众汽车以及臻驱科技董事长、总经理沈捷出席活动。
臻驱科技将与大众变速器天津公司在新能源车碳化硅功率半导体模块领域展开研发与产业化的全面合作，夯实大众电动化核心零部件的本土供应链布局。
长期以来，臻驱科技与大众汽车集团保持多层次技术协同，持续围绕电驱动、混动双电控等前沿技术开展联合攻关。本次围绕着功率模块的深度合作，将推动双方迈向产业链更深层次协同。未来，双方将进一步挖掘技术合作空间，围绕SiC模块、功率转、先进电驱方案等持续联合创新，共同推动高性能新能源动力解决方案的落地与持续升级。
派恩杰全国首发碳化硅铜互连封装工艺
近日，派恩杰半导体正式发布全国首款基于八英寸晶圆的碳化硅（SiC）铜互连封装工艺，标志着我国在功率半导体先进封装领域取得关键突破。
针对传统铝互连热膨胀系数与SiC失配、制约器件性能释放的行业痛点，派恩杰首创“顶部厚铜工艺”：在八英寸SiC晶圆制造阶段直接形成厚铜金属化层，替代传统多步异质金属化流程，将材料热膨胀系数差异缩小30%，工序由3步简化为1步。该技术可使芯片电流密度有望突破600A/cm²，功率循环寿命显著延长，同时为下一代嵌入式PCB封装奠定同质铜连接基础。
目前，派恩杰已围绕该技术构建起“顶部散热模块+铜互连+BGBM背面金属化”三大核心封装能力闭环，相关产品已大规模导入新能源乘用车及Tier-1动力平台。此次技术落地填补了国内SiC铜互连量产能力空白，将有力推动国产第三代半导体产业链整体竞争力提升。
曹操出行与大众交通签署战略合作协议
近日，曹操出行与大众交通正式签署战略合作协议，双方将围绕Robotaxi出行服务领域展开深度合作，依托各自资源优势共同探索上海及长三角区域Robotaxi规模化运营新模式，为智能网联汽车产业高质量发展注入新动能。
根据协议，双方将采用分阶段推进的合作模式：初期阶段，双方将联合启动Robotaxi示范运营，重点在运营资质申报、车辆全生命周期管理、平台系统对接、地面服务保障、安全运行体系等环节开展协同探索，积累运营经验；待政策环境与运营条件成熟后，双方将进一步扩大合作规模，推动规模化Robotaxi车队落地运营，持续打磨适配市场需求的商业模式与运营体系，全面提升智能出行服务能力。
在合作分工上，曹操出行将承担Robotaxi全栈解决方案及技术体系建设的主导角色，充分发挥其在车载智能设备研发、智慧运营管理体系建设等领域的技术积累；大众交通则将依托深耕城市交通运营多年的资源禀赋，以及在车辆精细化管理、本地化服务网络搭建方面的优势，与曹操出行共同构建标准化、高品质的Robotaxi服务体系，探索适配未来智能出行趋势的创新运营模式。

【NE数据】2026上半年DHT、双电控装机量：联合电子双电控产量突破10万！
NE时代根据新能源乘用车终端数据统计，2026上半年中国新能源乘用车插混车DHT系统装机量为124万套，同比下降-26.55%。双电控装机量达到123万，同比下降-24.54%。
■ DHT方面，装机下滑一方面受到新能源市场结构变化影响——上半年新能源汽车销量仍超过744万辆，但纯电动车占比已升至67%，混动系统需要与持续扩大的纯电市场争夺增量；另一方面，2026年起享受购置税减免的插混及增程车型，等效纯电续航门槛提高至100公里，同时对馈电油耗、电耗提出更高要求，推动部分旧平台和短续航车型退出，放大了产品切换期的装机波动。
■ 双电控方面，星驱科技同比增长超过500%，是双电控市场最大的结构性变量。联合电子同比增长也超过500%，全新一代双电控累计产量突破10万套。智新控制同比增长62.7%、伊控动力同比增长175.0%、富奥股份增长58.8%。
PS：该数据是NE时代根据国内整车终端销售数据为统计口径整理，不含进出口数据，统计结果可能会与相关零部件企业的实际出货数据存在差异。
鉴于部分企业的业务模式具有独特性，当前的数据统计方式难以全面、精准地反映其业务规模，故而这部分企业的排名未予体现。如有疑问，请扫描文末二维码联系我们。
新能源整车与零部件的供配关系时常变动，如有疏漏，欢迎相关企业联系指正。

title: Jim Bureau: Building Resilience Amid Ongoing Climate Risk
content:
Jim Bureau: Building Resilience Amid Ongoing Climate Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
Jim Bureau, CEO of Loftware, talks to Supply Chain Digital about the supply chain risk of El Niño. Credit: Loftware
In a time defined by ongoing extreme climate events, Jim Bureau, CEO of Loftware, explores how businesses are responding to growing geopolitical disruption
In recent years, major climate events have become more and more regular, causing disruption to supply chain operations around the world. Inconsistencies with rainfall and drought have caused crops, including cocoa beans, coffee beans and
– the leaves behind matcha – to fail.
Now, extreme and unseasonable temperatures have sparked wildfires around the world. Events which were once a disruptive but rare occurrence have now become a common feat. As a result, organisations around the world are having to learn how operate alongside them, instead of reacting to them.
Loftware helps more than 16,000 organisations manage supply chain risk amid ongoing complexity, through its improved collaboration and visibility. Loftware's solutions provide greater agility to changing conditions and significant aid with compliance.
Supply Chain Digital spoke to Jim Bureau, the CEO of Loftware, about ongoing climate events could become the latest global supply chain shock, disrupting trade flows, business operations and
food production
How has extreme weather impacted global supply chains?
Extreme weather has become
more than a seasonal disruption
; it's changing how supply chains operate. Recent heatwaves across Europe affected transport networks, inland shipping, energy infrastructure, agricultural production and labour availability simultaneously. Because today's supply chains are highly interconnected, disruption in one region quickly creates knock-on effects across manufacturing, logistics, inventory and customer fulfilment around the world.
The assumption can no longer be that disruption is temporary. Businesses need to plan for volatility as a constant rather than the exception.
How are climate events forcing businesses around the world to rethink their sourcing strategies and supplier diversification?
Many organisations are moving away from relying heavily on a single supplier, region or transport route. Diversification is becoming essential, but adding suppliers also adds complexity.
The challenge isn't simply finding alternative sources. It's ensuring every supplier, manufacturer and logistics partner has access to accurate product information, labelling requirements and compliance data. Without that
shared visibility
, diversification can introduce as much risk as it removes.
Heatwaves across Europe have led to major wildfires. Credit: Getty Images
How is disruption at shipping and trade chokepoints impacting global supply chains?
Whether it's low river levels restricting inland shipping, ports operating below capacity or delays at major trade routes, chokepoints create ripple effects throughout the supply chain. Companies often have to reroute shipments, change production schedules or source products differently at short notice.
The organisations that respond most effectively are those that can make informed decisions quickly because they have real-time connected data and close collaboration across their entire supply chain network.
What can organisations do to ensure they remain operable amid disruption and last-minute changes?
Resilience today depends less on having
bigger stockpiles
and more on having better information. Businesses need real-time visibility across suppliers, manufacturing sites, logistics providers and customers so they can respond quickly without sacrificing compliance or accuracy.
But visibility alone isn't enough. Organisations also need the ability to execute changes consistently across their entire supply chain. When production shifts to a new facility, an alternative supplier is onboarded or products are redirected to a different market, every label, packaging specification, language requirement and regulatory declaration needs to be updated accurately and immediately.
That's why product identification has become a strategic capability rather than an operational afterthought. Companies that centralise and standardise product identification while enabling secure collaboration across trading partners can adapt far more quickly, reduce the risk of errors and keep products moving, even as conditions change around them.
Digital platforms can help increase visibility and resilience. Credit: Getty Images
What can supply chains learn about resilience following ongoing disruption?
The biggest lesson is that resilience is no longer about recovering after disruption; it's about operating effectively despite it.
That requires stronger collaboration across the supply chain, trusted product data and digital platforms that allow organisations to coordinate decisions in real time.
Climate events
, geopolitical uncertainty and regulatory change are all increasing pressure on global operations, but businesses that build better connected supply chain ecosystems will be far better positioned to adapt.
Ultimately, resilience isn't measured by how rarely disruption occurs. It's measured by how confidently an organisation can respond when it does.

title: Nissin Foods Turns to Blue Yonder for Smarter Supply Chains
content:
Nissin Foods Turns to Blue Yonder for Smarter Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Nissin Foods has partnered with Blue Yonder and Highspring to transform its supply chain planning. Credit: Nissin Foods
Nissin Foods is digitising its supply chain planning amid ongoing market volatility, turning towards expertise from Blue Yonder and Highspring
Nissin Foods USA has announced its partnership with
Blue Yonder
and Highspring in order to undertake a digital transformation.
The company is overhauling its supply chain management, moving away from legacy tools and towards greater integration and flexibility.
Through this, Nissin will be able to respond better to changing demand, improve product availability and reduce costs.
Navigating complexity
In today's world, supply chains operating on manual spreadsheets and legacy systems are susceptible to risk. Across the industry, companies are facing ongoing supply chain challenges, with talent shortages, ageing workforces and rising operational complexity.
To mitigate the fallout, Nissin Foods is turning to Blue Yonder and Highspring to transform its demand and supply planning capabilities. Nissin Foods was founded in 1958, by the inventor of the first instant ramen noodle in Japan. In 1972, the brand opened itself up to American consumers, with Cup Noodles debuting in the US a year later. The company develops a vast portfolio of Asian-inspired meals, with a focus on taste and affordability.
As supply chains grow more dynamic, organisations need advanced planning capabilities that can adapt continuously to changing market conditions.
Ann Marie Jonkman, Vice President, Products & Services at Blue Yonder
Now, it is looking to modernise its supply chain operations, turning towards Highspring and Blue Yonder to do so. Highspring, a leading global services provider, and Blue Yonder, an AI company focused on end-to-end digital supply chain transformation, will be
using AI
and machine learning to ensure Nissin can implement a fully-integrated AI-powered supply chain solution.
Highspring's supply chain-as-a-service offering is helping Nissin Foods unlock the potential to operate using unbiased, accurate and data-driven planning capabilities. Through this, the food brand will be better adept at streamlining inventory management, reduce operational costs and improve forecasting accuracy. At the same time, Nissin will be able to predict operational expenses much more accurately.
“We look forward to collaborating and embarking on this journey to help Nissin because it's vital for organisations to have the right capabilities to enable a more dynamic and resilient supply chain,” says Bob Patel, Managing Partner and Practice Leader, Retail Planning and
Supply Chain Management
at Highspring.
Bob Patel, Managing Partner and Practice Leader at Highspring
“With AI- and ML-driven innovation from Blue Yonder and Highspring’s deep domain experience coupled with unique supply chain-as-a-service, we look forward to serving Nissin Foods in its vision to improve its operational efficiency, improve forecast accuracy and make better planning decisions, allowing Nissin to focus on its core competency by offering an innovative variety of products at a faster pace.”
Improving accuracy
Highspring combines collaboration and strategy with tailored solutions for each company, ensuring it offers strong expertise to help organisations grow. It makes use of AI, data, governance, risk and compliance in order to drive widespread transformation.
Agility is needed in the consumer goods industry, as social media plays a major role in demand. Moreover, ongoing disruption such as climate events impact crops and food supply chains now more than ever. Highspring's expertise helps organisations in the consumer goods industry face ongoing disruption with fast and long-lasting strategies which help them
stay resilient
amid rising costs, demand shifts and changing customer preferences.
Blue Yonder's supply chain planning capabilities can drive 95% improved forecast accuracy, 60% increased planning efficiency and up to 30% less inventory expenses. It helps organisations evaluate scenarios and quantify business impact with integrated planning across supply chain operations.
“As supply chains grow more dynamic, organisations need advanced planning capabilities that can adapt continuously to changing market conditions,” explains Ann Marie Jonkman, Vice President, Products & Services at Blue Yonder.
Ann Marie Jonkman, Vice President, Products & Services at Blue Yonder
“Together with Highspring, we’re helping Nissin Foods unify demand and supply planning and align operations with corporate goals so they can improve forecast accuracy, optimise resources, reduce waste and make faster, more informed decisions across their entire enterprise and network.”
Supply chain resilience
Blue Yonder's Demand and Supply Planning solution is a cognitive, AI-powered feature which includes an intelligent optimisation solver. This will help Nissin Foods to better manage its inventory levels, ensuring all resources are being used accurately and to their full potential.
It helps develop
supply chain resilience
through the automated forecasting, which also translates to reduced working capital. Real time insights help increase agility across workflows, meaning teams can respond better to changes without disrupting operations.
"Since Nissin Foods founder Momofuku Ando invented the world's first instant ramen and sparked a global food revolution, innovation has been the foundation of our success,” says Yukio Yokoyama, Chief Representative, Americas, President and CEO of Nissin Foods.
Yukio Yokoyama, Chief Representative, Americas, President and CEO of Nissin Foods
“This latest transformation, through our partnership with
Blue Yonder
, represents the next chapter in that legacy, empowering us with enhanced visibility, agility and collaboration across our supply chain, finance and operations teams. By leveraging advanced planning capabilities, we will be able to make smarter decisions, respond more quickly to market changes and operate more efficiently across our business.
"Just as importantly, this transformation will strengthen our partnerships with customers by helping us better serve their needs, anticipate changing demand and adapt to evolving consumer preferences, ensuring we continue to deliver the quality, reliability and value they expect from Nissin Foods."

title: RapidRatings: Turning Supply Chain Risk Into Resilience
content:
RapidRatings: Turning Supply Chain Risk Into Resilience
Prioritise Us
on Google
Watch this on-demand webinar to hear how leading organisations are turning turbulence into resilience. Credit: Getty
Watch an on-demand webinar to gain insights from Tom Derry and James Gellert about how leading companies are navigating ongoing supply chain risk
Supply chain turbulence has been rife in recent years, driven by changing legislation and rising volatility. Tom Derry, former CEO of ISM and James Gellert, Executive Chair of
RapidRatings
, know this risk all too well.
In an on-demand webinar, Tom and James explore how teams navigate constant disruption, financial vulnerability and the collapse of globalisation's consensus in modern supply networks.
Their discussion examines how procurement organisations navigate an environment where disruption has become normal rather than exceptional.
now on-demand.
Evolution of globalisation assumptions
Tom became CEO of ISM in 2012. According to Tom, the organisation operated under assumptions that had existed for nearly 20 years, from the mid nineties to the mid 2010s.
"I use Brexit as my milestone event, because it signalled that the consensus around the benefits of globalisation and open country markets was beginning to fragment — that there were risks associated with it," says Tom.
Tom Derry, former CEO of ISM (Credit: ISM)
Over the next decade, ISM witnessed the unravelling of the globalisation consensus. The COVID-19 pandemic followed, then a series of geopolitical tensions that did not exist before.
James brings expertise from corporate finance and risk. Before RapidRatings, he built and ran three companies in data, analytics and technology, having started as a banker focused on credit and fixed income.
RapidRatings works with clients across roughly 27 industries. The company exposes financial
vulnerabilities
hiding within supply networks that rarely appear until it is too late, and that link directly to operational and reputational risks procurement teams are judged on.
RapidRatings 2025 findings:
85% of enterprises experienced increased costs
42% experienced production disruptions due to supply chain issues, and a quarter experienced quality issues
81% of enterprises experienced disruptions of one kind or another in their supply chain, yet their suppliers themselves reported a lower rate of impact
Decision making in permacrisis
Supply chain and procurement teams are responding to challenges that arrive faster and with greater impact than before.
According to James
, much of what the industry faces today ties back to the concept of permacrisis.
Factors include the interest rate environment, the macroeconomic environment, managing working capital, private credit, private equity, the capital markets and geopolitical and economic risks.
"It used to be the case that you were doing your job well if product showed up on time and in full. That's how performance was measured. That began to change during the pandemic, and it's certainly the case today," says Tom.
"It's no longer enough to say your product arrived on time and the quality was good. These existential factors for the company are now being evaluated, and you're being evaluated on them. That's a real change."
Performance measurement has expanded beyond traditional delivery metrics. Procurement professionals now face accountability for factors that affect company survival.
Financial health as predictor
Financial health is a foundational indicator of how well positioned a company is to meet its obligations. Historically, many businesses and supply chain organisations have worked in silos, with different people looking at financial risk,
cybersecurity risk
, ESG and governance factors, and more traditional measures like quality and delivery.
"Ultimately, though, a company's financial health is a leading indicator of whether it can meet all of those other obligations, or whether it's presenting new risks in those areas that it wasn't before," says James.
There's been a change in the fundamental way of thinking — not just in the United States, but around the world — and in the policies countries are using to gain advantage in the global commercial game.
Watch On-Demand
James describes a K-shaped economy pattern in the corporate world. Companies doing well tend to be the larger, public ones. Companies doing less well tend to be middle market and private, because they act as the shock absorbers for supply chains.
"If I were in the audience thinking about my own supply base, my first instinct might be to assume it isn't in that kind of distress. I'd challenge that assumption — there are undoubtedly examples in your supply base; you just need to go and find them, and ask the tough questions if you haven't already," says Tom.
Tom compares the situation to an individual living paycheque to paycheque, making only minimum payments on credit cards without reducing actual debt. "That's not sustainable for me as an individual, and it's equally true for companies. I think we underestimate how much
stress exists in the supply base
Criticality beyond spend levels
A common mistake in supply chain risk management is ignoring apparently low levels of spend. Tom gives an example of a pharmaceutical company where the coating on a tablet represented an inconsequential level of spend for the company, but it supported US$2bn in revenue.
James Gellert, Executive Chair of RapidRatings (Credit: BizClik Media)
"Without that coating, they couldn't sell the product. So don't segment purely by level of spend — think about risk in terms of how much revenue and sales a given supplier supports, and
assess your risk
According to James, criticality is not the same as spend. Criticality can be measured in different ways.
"For me, the most important thing organisations can do is share information across risk domains and mandate that coordination, because a problem in financial health is often a leading indicator of problems elsewhere. You can't work in silos anymore," James adds.
The conversation between Tom and James is available to watch on demand. Their combined experience in procurement policy and corporate finance could provide insight for organisations navigating instability in supplier networks.

title: 81 years of Hiroshima bombing: Japan warns against cost of nuclear war
content: Japan has marked the 81st anniversary of the Hiroshima atomic bombing with renewed calls for a world free of nuclear weapons, as leaders and survivors warned that the lessons of 1945 remain increasingly relevant amid growing geopolitical tensions and renewed debate over nuclear deterrence.Thousands gathered at Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park on Wednesday morning to commemorate the world’s first wartime use of an atomic weapon. Representatives from more than 120 countries and regions joined survivors, government officials, and residents for the annual ceremony, where a minute of silence was observed at 8:15 a.m., the exact time the US B-29 bomber Enola Gay dropped the uranium bomb Little Boy over the city on August 6, 1945.An updated register containing the names of 353,639 atomic bomb victims was placed inside the park’s cenotaph, as Japan once again remembered those who lost their lives while urging the international community not to forget the devastating humanitarian consequences of nuclear war.Remembering the human costThe bombing destroyed much of Hiroshima within seconds. By the end of 1945, an estimated 140,000 people had died from the blast, severe burns, and radiation exposure. Three days later, the Fat Man plutonium bomb devastated Nagasaki before Japan announced its surrender on August 15, bringing World War II to a close.For many survivors, however, the suffering continued long after the war ended. Thousands of hibakusha, survivors of the atomic bombings, spent decades living with cancers, chronic illnesses, and other long-term effects linked to radiation exposure. They also became some of the world’s most prominent advocates for nuclear disarmament. According to Japanese government figures cited during this year’s ceremony, around 91,000 hibakusha remain alive today, with an average age of 86, underscoring the urgency of preserving their testimonies as the generation that witnessed the bombings continues to diminish.A message aimed at today’s worldThis year’s commemoration came against the backdrop of rising international tensions and renewed debate over nuclear deterrence.In his annual Peace Declaration, Hiroshima Mayor Kazumi Matsui warned that attempts to justify nuclear weapons as instruments of security risk repeating the tragedies of the past. “Downplaying the inhumanity of nuclear weapons and accepting the use of force to pursue one’s own prosperity risk cycles of violent retaliation that could ultimately result in another Hiroshima or Nagasaki,” Matsui said.He argued that too many political leaders continue to view nuclear deterrence as a realistic security strategy, a mindset he said pushes the goal of a world free of nuclear weapons further out of reach. Matsui also urged younger generations to learn from history and take an active role in promoting peace.Nuclear policy remains under scrutinyPrime Minister Sanae Takaichi also addressed the ceremony, emphasizing Japan’s commitment to its long-standing non-nuclear principles while renewing calls for global nuclear disarmament.At the same time, Japan’s nuclear policy remains the subject of domestic debate. Takaichi has previously expressed support for reviewing the country’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles, including the provision that prohibits the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japan. While she said Japan has upheld those principles since World War II, she stopped short of explicitly committing to maintain the current policy indefinitely.The discussion comes as concerns over nuclear security have intensified worldwide, with arms-control agreements weakening and several major powers continuing to modernize their nuclear arsenals.A warning that still resonatesMore than eight decades after the bombing, Hiroshima’s annual memorial continues to serve as both a tribute to those who lost their lives and a reminder of the consequences of nuclear conflict.As the number of living hibakusha steadily declines, the responsibility for preserving their experiences increasingly shifts to future generations. The ceremony’s message remains as relevant today as it was decades ago: while technology, politics, and global alliances may change, the humanitarian consequences of nuclear war remain unchanged—and should never be forgotten.

title: Boeing's 300-nautical-mile JDAM LR strike weapon enters production
content: The U.S. Air Force has cleared Boeing’s GBU-75 Joint Direct Attack Munition Long Range (JDAM LR) for initial production, marking a significant step toward fielding an affordable long-range precision weapon capable of striking targets more than 300 nautical miles (555 km) away.The Air Force awarded Boeing a $75 million Undefinitized Contract Action (UCA) for production of the BSU-111/B Payload Delivery Unit (PDU), following nearly $100 million in company-funded development. According to Boeing, the initial production will support the U.S. Navy, which has been evaluating the weapon as a low-cost stand-off strike capability.Turning a familiar bomb into a long-range strike weaponThe JDAM family has been one of the world’s most widely used precision-guided munition systems since entering service in 1999, converting conventional unguided bombs into GPS/INS-guided weapons with high accuracy. A standard JDAM typically has a range of around 15 nautical miles, while the JDAM Extended Range (ER) variant uses deployable wings to extend that to roughly 40 nautical miles.The JDAM LR pushes that concept much further. Instead of relying solely on glide, the weapon combines the familiar JDAM guidance kit, deployable wing kit, and aircraft interface with a compact turbojet engine, effectively transforming the weapon into a powered, cruise missile-like munition while retaining compatibility with existing JDAM-equipped aircraft. Boeing says the configuration enables the weapon to travel more than 300 nautical miles carrying a 500-pound (226-kilogram) payload.Designed to bridge the gap between bombs and cruise missilesOne of the JDAM LR’s biggest selling points is affordability. Rather than developing an entirely new missile, Boeing designed the weapon to leverage the existing JDAM ecosystem already used by the U.S. military and numerous allied air forces. This allows aircraft already certified to carry conventional JDAMs to integrate the long-range version with comparatively limited changes while enabling production at significantly higher volumes than many dedicated stand-off missiles.According to Boeing, the weapon is intended for precision land attack, maritime strike, and aerial mining missions, allowing aircraft to engage targets from well outside the effective range of many modern air defense systems. The company has described the JDAM LR as a system designed to supplement inventories of more expensive cruise missiles by providing a high-volume precision-strike option.Flight testing already underwayThe production decision follows a series of successful flight demonstrations conducted by the U.S. Navy earlier this year.In April, F/A-18 Super Hornets carried out two test flights over the Point Mugu Sea Range off the California coast, successfully demonstrating safe separation from the aircraft, powered flight, and precision navigation. According to the U.S. Navy, each demonstration traveled more than 200 nautical miles while maintaining guidance throughout the mission profile. Boeing later confirmed that the system has also demonstrated military-code GPS navigation and successful powered flight during testing.Why it mattersLong-range precision strike has become increasingly important as modern air-defense networks grow more capable, forcing aircraft to launch weapons from greater distances.Rather than replacing high-end cruise missiles, the GBU-75 JDAM LR is designed to complement them by offering a less expensive weapon that can be manufactured at scale while using much of the infrastructure already built around the existing JDAM family. If the program proceeds as planned, it could provide U.S. and allied forces with a significantly larger inventory of stand-off precision weapons capable of engaging land and maritime targets while keeping launch aircraft farther from contested airspace.

title: China's new tech can plan mass strikes to hit hundreds of targets
content: China is integrating artificial intelligence into its military operations with the introduction of an AI-powered system designed to assist in planning and coordinating large-scale air strike missions, according to a report.The technology has been developed to support military commanders during complex exercises involving numerous aircraft, targets, and weapons, allowing them to prepare battle plans more quickly and efficiently, as per the report. The system reflects China’s broader strategy of incorporating advanced digital technologies into modern warfare.Newly developed AI platform functions as a decision-support toolThe newly developed AI platform functions as a decision-support tool rather than an autonomous weapon. It processes large volumes of battlefield information, evaluates mission objectives, and recommends coordinated attack plans based on available aircraft, weapon systems, and operational constraints. By automating time-consuming planning tasks, the system enables commanders to respond more rapidly to changing battlefield conditions while maintaining human oversight over critical decisions.AI could assist decision-making by calculating battlefield developments in real time, assigning the most suitable targets to different weapons and determining when munitions should be used, according to the report.Ability to coordinate simultaneous attacks on hundreds of targetsOne of the system’s primary strengths is its ability to coordinate simultaneous attacks on hundreds of targets. Modern air operations often require multiple aircraft to strike different objectives at precisely coordinated times while avoiding conflicts in airspace and ensuring efficient use of resources. The AI can rapidly calculate flight routes, assign targets, recommend weapon allocation, and adjust operational plans if new intelligence or unexpected threats emerge during a mission. This capability can significantly reduce planning time compared with traditional manual methods.The development highlights the increasing role of artificial intelligence in military command and control. Around the world, armed forces are exploring AI applications for intelligence analysis, logistics, surveillance, battlefield management, and mission planning. AI systems are particularly valuable because they can process vast amounts of information in seconds, identify patterns that may not be immediately obvious to human analysts, and generate multiple operational options for commanders to evaluate.Despite these advantages, military experts emphasize that AI should complement rather than replace human decision-making. Combat environments are highly dynamic, and unexpected developments often require judgment, experience, and ethical considerations that current AI systems cannot fully replicate. Human commanders remain responsible for approving operational plans and making final decisions, especially in situations involving significant strategic or humanitarian consequences.China’s investment in AI-based military technologies reflects a broader global trend in defence modernization. Major military powers are increasingly focusing on intelligent command systems, autonomous platforms, and data-driven decision support to improve operational effectiveness. As advances in artificial intelligence continue, future military operations are expected to rely more heavily on AI-assisted planning while maintaining meaningful human control over the use of force.The introduction of this AI-assisted air strike planning system demonstrates how emerging technologies are reshaping military strategy. By combining rapid data analysis with human expertise, such systems have the potential to improve coordination, enhance operational efficiency, and support more informed decision-making in increasingly complex combat environments.

title: Firestorm Labs prints 1,000 parts, 12 drones aboard US Navy warship
content: Firestorm Labs has manufactured more than 1,000 components and assembled 12 Squall first-person-view drones aboard the USS Essex, demonstrating how military hardware could be produced during maritime operations. The two-week trial took place while the US Navy warship sailed from San Diego to Hawaii for RIMPAC 2026.Using its containerized xCell manufacturing platform, the US defense technology company produced drone components and repair parts despite waves reaching 12 feet. The deployment, organized through the Naval Postgraduate School CAMRE network and facilitated by FLEETWERX, aimed to reduce dependence on shore-based resupply while supporting repairs and combat readiness at sea.Manufacturing through rough seas on a warshipThe deployment was xCell’s first maritime demonstration under operational conditions. Instead of waiting for parts to be transported by aircraft, ship, or convoy, crews could manufacture equipment close to where it was required while remaining on station.Firestorm tested printer performance aboard the moving warship and produced three main categories of hardware: mechanical test pieces, components for Squall drones, and repair items requested by the crew.Operations continued in conditions reaching sea state 5, demonstrating production amid significant vessel movement.More than 20 crew-requested items were also manufactured. These included deck tie-down inspection gauges, reverse-engineered valve handwheels, electrical covers, cable hardware, door components, a Starlink deployment mount, and a nonconductive digging knife for explosive ordnance disposal teams.Protecting aircraft and supporting sailorsOne notable component was an Apache rotor guard droop stop designed during the first Army-Navy Apache operations conducted at sea. The device reduced the risk of the helicopter’s rotor striking the deck as the vessel moved through unusually heavy seas off Southern California.Firestorm said an Apache main rotor costs approximately $500,000, while damage from a blade striking the deck could cost $230,000 for each of its four blades. Manufacturing the protective component aboard the ship helped enable operations with the helicopter’s rotors mounted.The team also converted a sailor’s idea into a vacuum adapter for inflatable Life Preserving Units. Because no suitable connector was known to exist, Firestorm designed three versions for different vacuums and operating requirements.Drones move from ship to exerciseFirestorm assembled 12 Squall FPV drones during the voyage and later flew them at RIMPAC in Hawaii. Soldiers, sailors, and Marines received training in additive manufacturing, drone assembly, and flight operations.Marines from the 3rd Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion subsequently operated the drones as adversary aircraft during a three-day counter-UAS exercise at Makua Military Reservation on Oahu. The flights supported experimentation conducted for CAMRE during the multinational exercise.“The Indo-Pacific logistics problem is real, and most of the answers on offer live in a pitch deck,” said Dan Magy, CEO of Firestorm. “We printed flight-ready aircraft and the parts a crew actually needed, in the conditions they’d actually face. That’s what manufacturing at the edge looks like when it works,” he added. The demonstration indicates that deployable additive manufacturing could shorten repair timelines, keep vessels operational for longer, and allow US forces and allied partners to regenerate expendable drone capacity across contested maritime regions.

title: Humanoid robots need these key technologies to work like humans
content: Building a humanoid robot is becoming more achievable as advances in AI, actuators, sensors, and battery technology make sophisticated components increasingly accessible. A new guide from the ROBO Global Robotics and Automation Index outlines the core technologies required, grouping them into three key systems: the robot’s “brain,” “body,” and “energy” source. The guide explains how AI processors, cameras, precision actuators, and next-generation solid-state batteries work together to enable human-like movement, perception, and autonomy. It also highlights the rapid growth of the humanoid robotics market, with new commercial models and supporting technologies expanding opportunities for developers, manufacturers, and investors.Humanoid robot guideAdvances in AI, robotics hardware, and battery technology are making it increasingly feasible to build humanoid robots, according to the new guide released by ROBO. The guide outlines the essential technologies needed to create a humanoid robot, describing the system in terms of three core elements: the “brain,” the “body,” and the “energy” source.The report says the biggest advantage of humanoid robots lies in their human-like form. Because they are designed with the same basic structure as people, they can navigate environments built for humans and use existing tools and equipment without requiring extensive infrastructure changes. This allows them to perform a broad range of tasks, from household chores such as loading dishwashers and organizing rooms to industrial jobs including material handling and factory assembly.To operate safely alongside people, humanoid robots require advanced perception and computing capabilities. Their “brain” combines arrays of cameras, LiDAR sensors, and tactile sensors that continuously collect information about the surrounding environment. Cameras and LiDAR generate detailed three-dimensional maps that help the robot navigate obstacles, while touch sensors in robotic hands enable it to adjust grip strength when handling objects ranging from heavy cookware to delicate glassware.Processing this vast amount of sensor data requires powerful onboard computing. Specialized AI processors analyze information in real time, allowing the robot to recognize objects, plan movements, maintain balance, and respond quickly to changes in its surroundings. These chips effectively serve as the robot’s central nervous system, coordinating perception, decision-making, and motion.Humanoid supply chainThe guide also highlights the importance of advanced actuators, which function as the robot’s muscles and joints. Modern humanoids typically combine rotary actuators for circular movements in areas such as the shoulders and hips with linear actuators that replicate the push-and-pull action of human muscles. Many robotic joints also incorporate compact, high-torque gear systems such as harmonic drives, enabling precise, stable movements while supporting heavy loads without excessive vibration.Power remains one of the biggest engineering challenges for humanoid robots. Since larger batteries increase a robot’s weight and energy consumption, manufacturers are seeking ways to improve efficiency rather than simply increasing battery size. According to the report, many next-generation humanoids are being designed to recharge autonomously or even replace their own battery packs. Developers are also exploring solid-state batteries, which promise higher energy density and improved safety by replacing flammable liquid electrolytes with solid materials.The guide notes that the commercial humanoid robotics market is expanding rapidly, with dozens of new models entering development worldwide. Alongside robot manufacturers, demand is also growing for suppliers of AI chips, sensors, actuators, precision gearing, and advanced battery technologies. As humanoids move closer to widespread deployment in homes, factories, warehouses, and service industries, the report suggests that the broader supply chain supporting these technologies is expected to play an increasingly important role in the robotics industry’s growth.

title: Lunar helium-3 eyed as fuel for 50-MWe next-gen US fusion plant
content: Fusion energy company TAE Technologies has signed an agreement with privately funded natural-resource and lunar-development firm Black Moon Energy Corporation (BMEC) to secure a potential helium-3 fuel supply as it advances toward its first commercial fusion power plant.Under the agreement, BMEC would supply helium-3 to TAE and work with the company on commercial development. The deal is aimed at building a future fuel supply chain for fusion, an area that could become increasingly important as more fusion companies move from experimental machines toward power generation.TAE says the agreement gives it greater flexibility in choosing its fuel cycle. Many fusion machines are designed around deuterium and tritium, but TAE’s technology is intended to operate with different fuel options.“This agreement can facilitate our path to power by providing an alternative fuel supply option,” said TAE CEO Michl Binderbauer. “TAE has a high degree of flexibility to select from the most cost-competitive fuel cycle, whereas many other fusion machines are able to operate only on the deuterium-tritium cycle; this provides TAE’s technology with future flexibility, depending on how fuel markets change over the long-run.”A new fuel optionHelium-3 is a light isotope of helium that TAE sees as one possible fuel for its fusion technology. Securing a potential supplier now could help the company address one of the challenges of commercial fusion: developing a reliable fuel supply alongside the reactors themselves.Black Moon Energy is pursuing helium-3 resources through lunar development. The company plans to conduct a robotic lunar mission within five years to gather data and test the feasibility of a commercial-scale helium-3 production operation.“Developing a future supply chain for fusion fuels is a critical component of bringing fusion power to market,” said David Warden, CEO of Black Moon Energy Corporation. “By working with TAE, we are helping establish the commercial framework needed to support next-generation energy systems.”TAE has spent nearly three decades developing its fusion technology and has built five fusion machines. Its current-generation machine, Norm, is being used to advance the technology toward a commercial plant.The next major step is Da Vinci, TAE’s planned first fusion power plant. The company expects the facility to generate 50 megawatts of electricity, with a site expected to be selected later this year.From supply to powerTAE expects Da Vinci to begin operations in 2031. The company says future plants could scale to between 350 and 500 megawatts, potentially allowing the technology to move from a demonstration facility to larger commercial power generation.The helium-3 agreement does not mean TAE has secured a current commercial fuel supply. Instead, it establishes a prospective supply option and a framework for future collaboration as both companies develop their respective technologies.That distinction is important because commercial fusion will require more than a working reactor. Companies will also need fuel, equipment, manufacturing capacity, and supply chains capable of supporting repeated plant deployments.For TAE, the agreement adds another piece to that commercial roadmap while giving the company flexibility to evaluate fuel options as it moves toward Da Vinci and future fusion power plants.

title: Meta's Muse Spark 1.2 makes 1,000+ tool calls in 24-hour coding test
content:
The system can also coordinate multiple persistent background agents during a session. Instead of creating a new helper for every individual task, these agents remain active, carry out follow-up work and decide when to send information back to the main agent.
Meta says this approach is intended to reduce repeated information gathering, latency and the amount of user intervention required for multi-step engineering work.
Coding tasks that run longer

Releasing Muse Code in beta today. It's a terminal coding agent that takes on complete software engineering tasks across large repos: planning changes, writing code, validating the results. Powered by Muse Spark 1.2, a coding-focused model update.
