title: BYD files six more solid-state battery patents - electrive.com
content:
BYD has published six new patents covering key aspects of solid-state battery technology. The filings focus on improving the contact between electrodes and solid electrolytes as the company reportedly targets pilot production of dual-electrolyte cells in 2027.
Archive image: BYD's second-generation Blade Battery
Image: BYD
Four of the new patents concentrate on materials and cell chemistry. One proposes adding an ion-conducting, electrochemically stable interlayer between halide and sulphide electrolytes to prevent unwanted chemical reactions and extend cycle life. Another uses a first solid electrolyte as a buffer layer between the active cathode material and a sulphide electrolyte, aiming to improve stability while limiting heat generation. According to the patent, the active cathode layer should not release more than 117 joules per gram under thermal conditions.
Two further patents focus on the cathode structure itself. One describes a dual-layer composite cathode that combines monocrystalline and polycrystalline cathode materials with different solid electrolytes. BYD says the design seeks to combine the higher structural stability of monocrystalline materials with the superior rate performance of polycrystalline materials.
Another patent proposes a cathode based on three materials, in which lithiated metal oxides and metal sulphides are mixed with a solid electrolyte to reduce interfacial resistance, improve specific capacity and extend cycle life.
The remaining two patents move beyond materials science and towards manufacturing. One introduces ionic liquid wetting agents with a gradient distribution across the electrode to improve ion transport and maintain reliable contact between solid materials. The other defines a quality metric called ‘Re’ for the contact ratio between cathode and electrolyte particles. BYD states that at least 60 per cent of a cathode particle’s perimeter should be in contact with electrolyte particles to improve charging performance, capacity and durability.
The latest patents follow
a solid-state battery patent granted by the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) in late July
covering composite cathode structures. According to Chinese media, BYD plans to start small-scale production of solid-state cells using its dual-electrolyte cathode design in 2027. The first cells are expected to be evaluated in prototype vehicles before any wider deployment. BYD has not officially confirmed the reported production timeline.
These new reports build on the company’s previously disclosed solid-state battery roadmap. Last year, BYD
confirmed it had already produced its first solid-state battery cells
and planned demonstration vehicles from 2027 before targeting broader commercialisation towards the end of the decade. Earlier this year, the manufacturer also
revealed progress in both sodium-ion and solid-state battery research
, underlining its strategy of developing multiple next-generation battery chemistries in parallel.
While BYD continues to advance the technology, large-scale production remains a challenge across the industry. In June, CATL Chairman Robin Zeng cautioned that engineering and manufacturing constraints mean
solid-state batteries are still several years away from mass-market deployment
. Nevertheless, the technology remains a major focus for battery manufacturers.

title: CATL Expands Its Lead in the Global Battery Market - electrive.com

The global market for batteries used in electric and hybrid vehicles grew by 20 per cent in the first half of 2026. CATL increased its market share to around 40 per cent.
Third generation of the Shenxing battery from CATL

According to the latest analysis by South Korean market research firm SNE Research, global EV battery cell demand reached 608.5 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 20 per cent year on year. However, growth slowed compared to
the full year 2025
, when demand increased by 31.7 per cent. The analysis covers battery cells used in battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids.
CATL remained the market leader, with battery cell deliveries totalling 242.7 GWh in the first half of the year. The Chinese manufacturer increased deliveries by 25.3 per cent year on year, lifting its global market share from 38.2 to 39.9 per cent.

LG Energy Solution was the highest-ranked South Korean battery maker in third place. The company delivered 52.6 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 8.4 per cent year on year. However, its global market share fell from 9.6 to 8.6 per cent.
The top 10 battery suppliers for electric and hybrid vehicles in the first half of 2026 comprised seven Chinese manufacturers – CATL, BYD, CALB, Gotion, EVE, SVOLT and Sunwoda – alongside South Korea’s LG Energy Solution and SK On, and Japan’s Panasonic.

title: 'World's first embodied all-terrain' humanoid robot Lumo unveiled
content: DOBOT has unveiled LUMO, describing it as the world’s first embodied all-terrain humanoid robot designed to operate across a wide range of environments and roles. The robot is built to move seamlessly through homes, shopping malls, schools, and other indoor spaces while adapting its behavior for different users and tasks. Combining vision, voice, and motion capabilities, LUMO can actively perceive its surroundings and respond without relying solely on commands. The system is also designed to learn from user interactions continuously, improving its performance over time and positioning humanoid robots as long-term companions for everyday life, education, and interactive applications.Recently, Dobot remotely operated its Atom humanoid robot from 1,118 miles (1,800 kilometers) away using virtual reality, demonstrating it cooking a steak with human-like precision.DOBOT humanoid targets homesLUMO is described as the world’s first embodied all-terrain humanoid robot designed to operate across a wide range of everyday environments while adapting to different users and applications. DOBOT showcased LUMO navigating grass, sand, and cobblestones with a smooth, human-like gait while transitioning seamlessly between outdoor, home and office environments. The humanoid demonstrated boxing, dancing and backflip capabilities, along with emotion recognition and proactive companionship. It also adjusted its movements by switching to a quieter walking mode and turning off lights after detecting its owner had fallen asleep. The demonstration, filmed without visual effects, highlighted LUMO’s intelligent interaction, mobility and consumer-focused design, reports Eu.36kr. View this post on Instagram Standing nearly 1.3 meters (4.3 feet) tall, DOBOT LUMO features a friendly, approachable design and natural, intuitive interactions aimed at supporting a wide range of users. Unlike conventional robots that are typically built for a single task or location, LUMO is designed to move freely between multiple indoor environments and perform a variety of roles depending on the needs of its users. The robot combines computer vision, voice interaction, and motion control to perceive its surroundings, communicate naturally, and carry out actions without relying solely on predefined commands. This multimodal approach allows the humanoid to respond to changes in its environment while interacting with people in a more intuitive way. DOBOT says LUMO is capable of switching between functions such as a household companion, educational assistant, sports playmate and science-learning partner, making it suitable for both personal and educational use.Robots learn peopleThe company also highlights the robot’s ability to continuously learn from user interactions, enabling it to improve its responses and adapt its behavior over time. Rather than acting only as a command-driven machine, LUMO is designed to build familiarity with users through long-term engagement, offering increasingly personalized assistance as it gathers experience.Potential applications include classroom instruction, STEM education, interactive exhibits at museums and science centers, customer engagement in shopping malls, public information services, and home companionship. While DOBOT has emphasized LUMO’s artificial intelligence capabilities and user-focused design philosophy, the company has yet to release detailed hardware specifications such as the robot’s height, weight, degrees of freedom, payload capacity, walking speed, battery life, or onboard computing platform. The unveiling reflects a broader trend in the robotics industry, where developers are increasingly shifting their focus from factory automation to general-purpose humanoid robots capable of operating safely alongside people in everyday environments, reports Eu.36kr.With LUMO, DOBOT aims to position humanoid robots as intelligent companions that can integrate into daily life, support education, provide interactive services, and evolve alongside users through continuous learning and real-world experience.

title: 150-mile strike range gives tiny 670-ton warship oversized firepower
content: The United Arab Emirates Navy’s Falaj 3-class offshore patrol vessel is drawing attention for packing unusually heavy firepower into a hull displacing only around 670 tons.Built by Abu Dhabi Ship Building, a subsidiary of EDGE Group, the roughly 200-foot vessel combines anti-ship missiles, layered air defenses, guided rockets, remote weapon stations, and a modern 76mm naval gun. The design is intended for operations in the Persian Gulf, where ships may face drones, missiles, helicopters, and swarms of fast-attack craft at relatively short ranges.The first vessel of the class, Altaf, entered service in February 2025. Despite being officially classified as an offshore patrol vessel, the Falaj 3 carries weapons more commonly associated with missile corvettes.Layered air defense on a small hullAt the bow, the vessel carries a Leonardo 76mm OTO Super Rapid gun equipped with the STRALES guided ammunition system.The gun can fire DART guided projectiles against surface and aerial targets. The rounds are guided by a radio beam and use a proximity fuze, making them suitable for engaging maneuvering missiles and fast-moving small boats.Behind the gun is an eight-cell vertical launch system for MBDA VL MICA surface-to-air missiles, providing air-defense coverage out to roughly 12 miles.Further aft, a 21-cell Mk 49 launcher carries RIM-116 Rolling Airframe Missiles, adding another independent defensive layer against incoming aircraft and missiles.Exocet adds long-range strike powerThe offensive fit is equally notable. Four MM40 Exocet Block 3C anti-ship missiles give the Falaj 3 the ability to strike surface targets at ranges of around 150 miles.The vessel also carries two 12-cell Low-cost Guided Imaging Rocket launchers. LOGIR uses infrared guidance and was developed primarily for maritime and coastal-defense roles. The rockets provide a cheaper option for engaging drones, uncrewed surface vessels and fast attack craft without using more expensive missiles.Two EOS R400-M 30mm remote weapon stations provide additional close-range firepower. Two 32-barrel Rheinmetall Multi Ammunition Soft-kill System launchers can deploy decoys to help defeat incoming guided weapons.Designed for Gulf warfareThe Falaj 3’s sensor suite centers on a Leonardo Kronos 3D multifunction radar housed inside the integrated mast. It also carries a SPYNEL infrared search-and-track system for passive detection of nearby threats. Together, these systems give the vessel air and surface surveillance alongside several layers of offensive and defensive firepower. That configuration reflects the operating environment of the Persian Gulf, where naval vessels can face anti-ship missiles, drones and fast attack craft with limited warning.Rather than prioritizing patrol endurance alone, the Falaj 3 concentrates combat capability into a compact platform. EDGE is also building eight vessels based on the same design for Kuwait, where they will be known as the Al Dorra class.The Falaj 3 reflects a broader naval trend in which compact sensors, missiles and combat systems are allowing smaller vessels to perform missions once reserved for much larger warships. Its compact arsenal makes the class an unusually heavily armed modern offshore patrol vessel optimized for littoral operations.

title: 41,000-ton Trump-class nuclear warship may top $275B, lead ship $23B
content: The US Navy is planning a new fleet of nuclear-powered battleships that could fundamentally change the cost and scale of modern naval warfare. According to a report by the Congressional Budget Office, building 15 of these Trump-class warships will cost an estimated $275 billion.The lead warship alone will cost around $23 billion to build. Once full production begins, later ships in the series will average about $18 billion each over their operational lifetime. The report was requested by Senator Jeff Merkley to evaluate how the new platform affects long-term military spending.If these plans move forward, the Navy’s yearly budget for surface warships will more than double. Annual spending will jump from $6.9 billion to $15.2 billion. Between 2027 and 2056, defense planners intend to buy 72 major warships. This total includes the 15 new battleships alongside 57 Arleigh Burke-class destroyers.A massive hullThe proposed warship, designated BBGN, can reportedly weigh 35,000-41,000 tons when fully loaded. That makes it the largest surface combatant designed for the Navy since World War II.To put that size in perspective, the new ship has more than double the mass of a Zumwalt-class destroyer. It is also 3.5 times larger than the Navy’s current workhorse, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer.Naval engineers need a hull of this size to supply raw power. Modern radar, lasers, and computing networks require immense electricity. A massive hull provides the physical space needed for nuclear reactors, heavy cooling units, and high-voltage power networks.Capable of carrying heavy weaponsThe design focuses heavily on long-range strike capability and energy-based defense systems. For standard missile operations, the warship features 128 Mark 41 vertical launch cells capable of firing anti-air and land-attack munitions. These are supplemented by four large-diameter launch tubes dedicated to Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missiles.“The Navy has stated that the ship would be equipped to carry the nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile, or SLCM-N,” said the report. This armament gives the warship more firepower than any American vessel outside of Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines.“Other elements would include large lasers, a rail gun, and a variety of defensive systems such as guns, smaller missiles, decoys, and optical dazzlers intended to counter and disrupt unmanned aerial systems,” added the report.Reducing long-term operational costsThe choice of propulsion is central to the design. A conventional gas-turbine engine would lower initial construction costs by about 13 percent. However, a nuclear reactor dramatically reduces long-term operational costs. Nuclear propulsion allows the ship to run indefinitely without refueling, while generating the constant electricity required by futuristic radar and laser weapons.Manufacturing will rely on a shared industrial network. Different shipyards across the country will fabricate individual sections of the hull. Workers will then transport these sections to HII Newport News Shipbuilding, where final assembly will take place in Drydock 12, the same drydock used to build Ford-class aircraft carriers. The Pentagon is requesting $1 billion in early funding for 2027, aiming to place the official order for the first battleship in 2028.

title: Altilium patented tech to reduce EV battery material costs by 20%
content: The UK’s push for electric vehicle supply chain sovereignty just gained critical legal teeth.Clean technology firm Altilium has been granted its first UK patent for its EcoCathode technology. It will transform spent EV battery scrap directly back into high-purity cathode materials.The decision by the UK Intellectual Property Office — awarding Patent No. GB2637908B for “Material Recovery Method and Use” — protects Altilium’s hydrometallurgical recycling method. Independent testing by Imperial College London confirmed that materials recovered using Altilium’s process match the quality of virgin mined minerals. It comes at a pivotal moment. As European electric vehicle adoption accelerates and stricter battery recycling rules loom, securing domestic access to critical minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt has shifted from an environmental goal to a national security priority.Closed-loop efficiencyTypically, electric vehicle battery recycling relied on a fragmented, carbon-heavy supply chain where spent cells were crushed into “black mass” and shipped thousands of miles overseas for energy-intensive refining. Altilium breaks this reliance by using a closed-loop hydrometallurgical process to recover and regenerate high-purity, battery-grade cathode materials locally within the UK. It would cut transport emissions, energy consumption, and dependence on imported critical minerals.The process has been validated at an industrial scale alongside leading automotive OEMs and the Advanced Propulsion Center.“This patent represents a significant milestone for Altilium and validates years of research and development into creating a truly circular supply chain for battery materials. Intellectual property is fundamental to our strategy as we scale our technology from pilot operations to commercial production,” said Dr Christian Marston, Co-Founder and COO of Altilium. Cutting out overseas refiningAltilium is expanding its intellectual property by advancing international patent applications across key global jurisdictions to lay the ground for future technology licensing opportunities. Domestically, this patented technology drives the company’s key infrastructure deployment, anchored by two primary facilities in the UK. The commercial rollout begins at the ACT3 Scale-Up Plant in Plymouth, which focuses on processing end-of-life battery scrap into battery-grade intermediate materials. Building on this foundation, the planned ACT4 Mega-Refinery will scale production up to commercial volume, manufacturing both cathode active materials (CAM) and anode active materials (AAM) to fulfill a significant share of the UK’s domestic battery supply needs.Planned for Teesside, ACT4 is designed to process 150,000 EV batteries per year. It is said to be enough to supply over 20% of the UK’s total CAM requirements by 2030 while creating more than 500 green jobs.This closed-loop recycling system secures critical minerals within Britain’s borders, providing automakers with a resilient, localized alternative to volatile global mining supply chains. Reprocessing spent energy storage directly into high-purity inputs turns depleted battery cells into clean power for the next generation of electric vehicles. The circular process cuts production costs for battery materials by approximately 20% compared to virgin materials, offering automotive manufacturers both sustainability and financial incentives.Beyond strengthening supply chain security, this domestic loop insulates manufacturers from international commodity price shocks and significantly cuts the environmental impact of raw material extraction.

title: China finds first strong evidence of mysterious new matter glueball
content: In a global first, researchers at the Institute of High Energy Physics (IHEP) in China have found experimental evidence to confirm the presence of a glueball, a new form of matter. The research findings were made at the Beijing Spectrometer III (BESIII) experiment, as part of an international collaboration headed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). The Standard Model of physics states that the building blocks of our universe, atoms, are made up of matter particles and force carriers. Matter particles, or fermions, named quarks, build up protons and neutrons, the positively and neutrally charged particles inside the atomic nucleus. A force carrier holds the quarks together; this carrier is called a gluon. Physicists have long held that gluons can also attract each other and bind together to form a glueball, an entirely new form of matter that is composed only of a force carrier. For the past five decades, multiple experiments have been carried out to prove the existence of a glueball. However, it was only in 2011 that scientists in China spotted a potential glueball candidate in the experiments conducted at the Beijing Spectrometer III (BES III). How was the glueball found? The BES III is a particle physics experiment of the IHEP designed to study quantum chromodynamics (QCD) further and look for physics beyond the Standard Model. The BES III experiment collects data emerging from the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider II (BEPC II), a circular collider with a circumference of 787 feet (240 m). Since the BEPC also produces a large number of J/ψ particles, whose decays are the best avenues for glueballs, researchers at the BES III have been looking for them since the experiment began nearly two decades ago. In 2011, the team first spotted a new particle that they referred to as X(2370). Over the next 13 years, they recorded decays of over 10 billion J/ψ particles to determine its spin-parity quantum number as 0⁻⁺. With the mass and quantum numbers of this new particle in complete agreement with predictions of a glueball, the researchers became more confident of actually calling it so. Why is it important? More recently, the researchers also found many new decay modes of X(2370) while also determining its ‘flavor-singlet’ nature, where they lack quark flavor signatures. This is the most important and defining characteristic of a glueball and establishes a complete chain of experimental evidence for a pseudoscalar glueball. This confirms the theoretical prediction that gluons can bind to each other and form an entirely new kind of matter. The discovery is also a direct test of the non-Abelian gauge structure in quantum chromodynamics (QCD), which also states that gluons are capable of attracting and binding each other, without the involvement of quarks. This is important, since it also helps establish that QCD is a correct theory and it has been validated at low energies. As the clearest experiment in over 50 years to have found the evidence for glueballs, the finding also demonstrates the importance of the BEPC II in studies of strong interactions. The research was presented at the International Conference of High Energy Physics in Brazil.

title: China turns on world-first 16 MW typhoon-resistant wind platform
content: China’s first tension-leg platform (TLP) floating wind farm entered operation on Thursday, marking a major step in deep-water renewable energy. According to a statement from China National Offshore Oil Corp (CNOOC), the 16-megawatt Haiyou Anlan platform has been connected to the Lufeng oilfield power grid and is supplying renewable electricity directly to offshore oil production.This project is China’s first TLP floating wind platform and the largest in the world by installed turbine capacity. It is located farther offshore and in deeper waters than any similar TLP wind facility. Built to handle Level 17 typhoons, the platform shows China’s progress in floating offshore wind technology and may help future deep-sea wind projects.Built for deep waters and extreme weatherHaiyou Anlan sits in the Pearl River Mouth Basin, about 124 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Shenzhen in Guangdong Province. The platform is in waters around 446 feet (136 meters) deep and about 85 miles (136 kilometers) from the coast.The structure is almost as tall as a 110-story building and holds a 16 MW typhoon-resistant wind turbine. According to CNOOC, the facility has been designed for a service life of 25 years while withstanding powerful Level 17 typhoons.When fully running, the platform should generate about 54 million kilowatt-hours of electricity each year for the Lufeng oilfield. This is expected to save around 15,000 cubic meters of fuel oil annually and reduce carbon dioxide emissions by about 35,000 metric tons.Floating design tackles offshore engineering challengesUnlike traditional offshore wind foundations that are fixed to the seabed, tension-leg platforms float on buoyant hulls held in place by vertical tendons anchored to the ocean floor. This design keeps the platform stable and limits movement from waves and currents.Compared to semi-submersible floating platforms, TLP systems use less steel for each megawatt of capacity, take up less sea space, and are more stable. Even with these benefits, the technology is still one of the hardest types of floating offshore wind to build because it needs very precise engineering and installation.Haiyou Anlan weighs about 7,800 tons and sweeps an area equal to roughly 7.5 standard soccer fields. CNOOC said it developed high-strength mooring systems, high-precision anchoring technology, and a multi-equipment construction system for the project. Engineers also used a three-dimensional sea condition simulation system to achieve millimeter-level underwater connections during installation.Experts see potential beyond coastal wind farmsLin Boqiang, director of the China Center for Energy Economics Research at Xiamen University that the project represents an important technological breakthrough and points to the future direction of offshore wind development, as reported by Global Times. Floating wind systems can move beyond the limits of nearshore development and access stronger wind resources in deeper and more distant waters. While the core technologies for large turbines and floating platforms are already mature in China, costs remain a main challenge.Lin said that the broader significance lies in expanding the supply of green electricity in eastern China. More than 80 percent of the country’s wind and solar resources are concentrated in western regions, while the main centers of electricity consumption are in the east. Developing offshore wind farther from the coast could therefore bring clean power closer to major demand centers and reduce reliance on long-distance transmission from western China.China is also expanding its wider green fuel industry. According to a report released Wednesday by the National Energy Administration, the country had about 8 million tons of oil equivalent in annual green fuel production capacity by the end of 2025, including green methanol, green ammonia, and sustainable aviation fuel.

title: China's new renewable power project could reshape its energy landscape
content:
Massive solar corridor
The massive solar corridor is expected to stretch across one of northern China’s largest deserts. Once completed, it will rank among the world’s largest solar
developments, producing enough electricity to power millions of homes and industries. The project forms a key part of China’s broader strategy to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and expand renewable energy capacity.
Deserts have traditionally been viewed as difficult environments with limited economic value. However, China’s planners see these sun-rich regions as ideal locations for large-scale solar farms. The abundant sunlight, wide-open land, and relatively low population density make desert areas particularly suitable for renewable energy
projects
Solar panels can also create environmental benefits
The Great Solar Wall seeks to do more than capture sunlight. Engineers believe the solar panels can also create environmental benefits by providing shade, reducing soil temperatures, and limiting moisture loss from the ground. These changes may encourage the growth of vegetation beneath and around the panels, helping stabilize loose sand and reduce the spread of
desertification
Researchers are also experimenting with planting drought-resistant grasses and shrubs around the installations. Over time, this combination of renewable energy infrastructure and ecological restoration could improve local biodiversity and make desert landscapes more resilient.
China has invested heavily in renewable energy over the past decade and has become the world’s largest producer of solar power. Projects such as the Great Solar Wall play an important role in helping the country diversify its energy mix while reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
Electricity generated in the desert will be transmitted through high-capacity power lines to major cities and industrial centres, where energy demand continues to grow. This approach allows China to take advantage of remote regions with abundant renewable resources while supplying cleaner
electricity
to densely populated areas.
The initiative also supports the country’s long-term climate commitments, including increasing the share of non-fossil fuels in its energy system and lowering carbon emissions.
One of the most distinctive features of the project is its focus on combining clean energy production with land restoration. Desertification has long posed environmental and economic challenges in northern China, contributing to sandstorms, soil degradation, and the loss of productive land.
Scientists continue to monitor how these changes affect local wildlife, soil quality, and water availability. Their findings could help shape similar projects in other arid regions around the world.
Despite its promise, the Great Solar Wall is not without obstacles. Building and maintaining enormous solar facilities in remote desert environments requires significant financial investment, advanced engineering, and reliable.

title: HII partners with robotics firms to automate U.S. Navy ship production
content: America’s largest military shipbuilder is making one of its biggest automation investments yet, announcing a performance-based agreement worth up to $900 million aimed at bringing advanced AI-powered robotics into U.S. Navy ship production.HII has signed long-term agreements with Path Robotics and GrayMatter Robotics to develop autonomous manufacturing systems capable of performing some of the most labor-intensive tasks involved in building warships. Rather than simply replacing existing production equipment, the partnership aims to create robotic systems that can adapt to the complexity and variability of naval shipbuilding. An industry where no two projects are exactly alike.Teaching robots to build warshipsUnlike automotive manufacturing, where robots often repeat identical tasks on standardized production lines, shipbuilding presents a far greater engineering challenge. Large steel structures vary in size, shape, and assembly sequence, requiring extensive welding, grinding, blasting, painting, inspection, and structural assembly. According to HII, the new initiative will use physical AI, combining robotics, sensors, machine vision, and autonomous decision-making, to enable machines to perform these tasks while adapting to changing production conditions.The companies say the goal is to develop automation capable of learning, improving, and operating in one of manufacturing’s most demanding environments.A performance-based approachThe agreement is structured differently from a conventional defense contract. Instead of immediately awarding production work, HII will make up to $900 million in shipbuilding work available over the next seven years, provided both robotics companies achieve a series of predefined manufacturing, technology, and production milestones.The first phase focuses on developing and qualifying autonomous production techniques that meet the stringent quality requirements of U.S. Navy shipbuilding. These include robotic welding, grinding, blasting, painting, inspection, and fabrication processes, which will eventually be integrated into automated production lines.If those systems demonstrate acceptable cost, schedule, and quality performance, HII plans to begin outsourcing production work through the new manufacturing network.Expanding America’s shipbuilding capacityBeyond introducing new technology, the program is intended to address a broader challenge facing the U.S. maritime industrial base. Capacity. HII expects to outsource more than 2.5 million hours of shipbuilding work during 2026, representing a 30% increase compared with 2025. The company is also expanding its distributed manufacturing network, allowing more structural sections of ships to be fabricated outside its primary shipyards before final assembly. Initially, robotic production will focus on smaller steel structures before gradually expanding to larger units and complete modules used across multiple naval platforms.Supporting the Navy’s future fleetAccording to HII, the automation technologies are being developed for use across a wide range of U.S. Navy programs, including aircraft carriers, nuclear-powered submarines, destroyers, amphibious assault ships, future frigates, and unmanned surface vessels.Because the systems are designed to work within HII’s distributed manufacturing strategy, production could eventually be shared among multiple facilities rather than concentrated entirely at major shipyards.The collaboration is part of HII’s broader High-Yield Production Robotics (HYPR) initiative, which seeks to combine robotics, autonomous manufacturing, and industrial AI to improve efficiency while strengthening America’s naval industrial base.Modern naval shipbuilding remains one of the world’s most labor-intensive manufacturing sectors, with skilled welding and fabrication workers in particularly high demand. While automation has transformed industries such as automotive manufacturing and electronics, shipbuilding has been slower to adopt robotics because of the size, complexity, and variability of its products. If successful, HII’s approach could demonstrate that advances in physical AI are mature enough to automate tasks once considered too complex for machines.

title: Houston launches mobile CNG fueling for commercial truck fleets
content: Commercial fleet operators could soon have a simpler way to switch from diesel to natural gas without investing in permanent fueling stations. A new managed mobile compressed natural gas (CNG) fueling service will deliver fuel directly to fleet depots, allowing operators to refuel on-site while avoiding the cost and time associated with building fixed infrastructure.The launch comes alongside a new CNG supply hub in Houston, Texas, which will support customers across the Gulf Coast. The facility has already secured a two-year agreement to fuel about 100 Class 8 natural gas trucks for a global logistics company, giving the site contracted demand before operations begin in the third quarter of 2026.Station-free fleet fuelingUnlike conventional fueling stations, the new service delivers CNG and renewable natural gas (RNG) directly to customer facilities. Fleet operators do not need pipeline access or permanent fueling equipment. Instead, the provider manages gas sourcing, compression, transportation, storage, and dispensing through a single service.The model targets fleets operating at least 10 natural gas trucks or those planning conversions of similar size. Operators can scale fueling capacity as additional vehicles enter service without making significant upfront infrastructure investments.For many commercial fleets, access to fueling has remained one of the biggest obstacles to adopting natural gas vehicles. Company executives believe bringing fuel directly to fleet yards could remove that barrier.“Fleet operators increasingly seek the operating economics of natural gas trucks, but access to fueling can be a barrier to adoption,” said Dan Messina, Vice President of Growth and Strategy. He added that the mobile service allows fleets to adopt natural gas vehicles “faster and with greater flexibility.”Houston hub expands reachHouston serves as the backbone of the new fueling program. The supply hub will initially support the 100-truck logistics fleet while also supplying industrial customers, utilities, transportation operators, energy infrastructure projects, and data centers across the Gulf Coast.According to Certarus President Dale Winger, Houston remains an important market because of its growing energy demand and customer base. He said the new hub will improve service for existing customers while creating opportunities to reach new industries that require dependable mobile gas delivery.Natural gas demand has increased among sectors where pipeline connections remain limited or temporary supply is needed. Mobile delivery gives customers access to fuel without waiting for new pipeline infrastructure.Heavy-duty trucking focusThe company expects the new service to help fleets lower diesel consumption, reduce operating costs, and minimize driver downtime through on-site fueling. Eliminating trips to public fueling stations could also improve route efficiency for commercial trucking operations.The platform relies on an existing North American network that includes what the company says is the continent’s largest fleet of CNG transport trailers, portable compression equipment, integrated gas supply assets, and proprietary pressure reduction systems.Certarus is also converting its own tractor fleet to natural gas, allowing it to gain operational experience with the same vehicle platforms used by commercial customers. That practical knowledge could help refine the mobile fueling model as more heavy-duty fleets evaluate alternatives to diesel across the United States.

title: Hyliion to deliver multi-megawatt KARNO power modules to US Navy
content: Austin, Texas-based Hyliion has been awarded a contract from the Office of Naval Research (ONR) to deliver two multi-megawatt KARNO power modules.The $41.7 million contract is for the company to design, develop, and deliver two KARNO units for validation in land and maritime applications at NAVSEA, Philadelphia. The units will be tested to see whether they meet the high power requirements of naval and land-based missions.“This contract accelerates the development of our multi-megawatt KARNO systems and expands the range of naval platforms the technology can support,” said Thomas Healy, Founder and CEO of Hyliion.Healy went on to add that the ONR has been a “tremendous partner” in advancing the KARNO technology, and the continued investment reflects the confidence they have in the platform.What is the KARNO power module?The KARNO power module relies on KARNO Core, which will use linear electric motors in a four-shaft system to generate electricity. The KARNO Core builds on the principles of the 200-year-old Stirling thermodynamic cycle.It is being built to provide clean electricity as per the demand. The linear generator turns heat into electricity using a flameless, low-temperature oxidation process. Its design promises ultra-low to zero emissions without the need for any additional emission treatments.The 200 kW linear generator will feature synchronized shafts working together to drive a thermodynamic cycle that uses heat to power linear piston movements. These movements generate electricity as the shaft, featuring a magnet array, moves through static copper coils at a high frequency, according to the company.The company also offers an 800 kW power module that will be used to meet the requirements of the new contract.The company says it uses additive manufacturing or 3D metal printing to unlock design opportunities for the KARNO Core. Hyliion says it is working with the ONR to deliver scalable, flexible power for U.S. Naval operations.US Navy’s interest in Hyliion’s techUnder the contract, Hyliion will develop and deliver two KARNO Power Modules rated at 2+ MW and 3+ MW scale. These systems build on the company’s modular 800 kW architecture to meet the higher power requirements of naval and land-based missions.The multi-megawatt KARNO Power Modules are expected to expand the capabilities that have driven Navy interest in the technology: fuel flexibility, high electrical efficiency, and a low-maintenance design optimized for demanding operating environments, according to a press release from the company.These attributes can reduce logistical burden, extend mission endurance, and deliver resilient power for maritime and expeditionary operations while maintaining low acoustic and thermal signatures.The KARNO Power Module is designed to power next-generation autonomous vessels, ensuring uninterrupted operations at sea with low maintenance and fuel consumption. Moreover, one of its key benefits is that it can leverage the available fuel infrastructure on site – ranging from diesel, R/CNG, propane, ammonia, methanol, gasoline, hydrogen, and more.The modules offer low heat signature and quiet operation, which enhances operational readiness and security. They also have fewer moving parts and an overall rugged design, which makes them well-suited to deliver power in challenging situations.The company says that the contract will allow it to mature the KARNO architecture across diverse markets. It aims to use the same scalable platform to serve both defense missions and high -growth distributed power applications, including data centers.

title: Lasers, custom paste unlock record efficiency TOPCon solar cells
content: A new study has improved the power conversion rate of Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact (TOPCon), which are an advanced type of silicon solar cell. Particularly, the dual-action metallization strategy pushed industrial TOPCon silicon cells to a certified power conversion efficiency of 26.31 percent. Typically, TOPCon solar cells lose efficiency during metallization because high-temperature firing damages the passivation layer and requires thick gridlines that block light. A new strategy pairing aluminum-free silver paste with laser-enhanced contact optimization (LECO) solves this by using precise laser activation instead of heat. The development comes from the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering (NIMTE) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences alongside Soochow University. “The new approach resolves the intrinsic trade-off between contact resistivity and passivation preservation without compromising manufacturability, providing a practical route toward the industrialization of next-generation high-efficiency photovoltaic technologies,” the team stated in the press statement. Double-edged sword of solar heatTOPCon solar panels dominate the global market because these can be manufactured on existing production lines with minimal retooling. But the high efficiency relies on an ultra-thin oxide cushion beneath the electrical contacts, which prevents captured electrons from recombining and preserves the energy absorbed from sunlight.The flaw was in the finish. Conventional manufacturing prints a silver-aluminum paste on the surface and fires the cell in a high-temperature furnace. The aluminum spikes downward. It bites through the protective passivation layer and deforms the silicon emitter beneath. To make matters worse, the runny paste spreads wide during firing, blocking precious incoming sunlight. The team prevented cell damage by pairing an aluminum-free silver paste with Laser-Enhanced Contact Optimization. Notably, the specialized, high-retention paste forms ultra-thin, tall gridlines with a 55 percent aspect ratio that eliminate aluminum spiking while reducing light shading.Meanwhile, single-frequency lasers under reverse voltage bias precisely weld low-resistance silver contacts at micro-sites. It replaces high-heat roasting and preserves the underlying crystal structure.Enabled by the custom paste, the crucial passivation layer are safeguarded from the severe lattice disruption and aluminum alloying damage caused by existing high-temperature firing.Highest current recorded Overall, the technique worked. The design yielded a record-breaking short-circuit current density of 41.98 mA/cm² by maximizing light absorption and preventing charge leakage.As per the researchers, this density is “the highest certified Jsc reported for large-area TOPCon solar cells to date.”The development shows that minimizing optical shading and protecting the passivation layer directly translates into maximum current extraction.Furthermore, the team says that the process could be easily integrated into existing assembly lines. Hence, it could avoid changing the expensive factory infrastructure. And bonus, it delivers a rare trifecta for solar energy: cheaper power, improved long-term stability, and maximum sunlight utilization.Factories, warehouses, logistics hubs, and office buildings depend on TOPCon panels to maximize energy yield within limited roof space. By producing more kilowatt-hours per square foot, these panels allow commercial properties to optimize long-term power generation across a 25- to 30-year operational lifespan.The study findings were published recently in the journal Matter on August 6.

title: New catalyst keeps 85% performance after 150,000 cycles, in H2 fuel cells
content: A newly unveiled catalyst architecture has been designed for low-temperature hydrogen fuel cells. The development could solve a long-standing compromise in clean energy tech: keeping expensive platinum catalysts stable without destroying their power output.In testing, the researchers led by Gang Wu at Washington University in St. Louis found that the catalyst maintains high performance with minimal precious metal content.Interestingly, the tech retained 85% of its performance after 150,000 voltage cycles (roughly equivalent to 25,000 hours of operation).“Our strategy is using this new carbon nanostructure to synthesize platinum cobalt intermetallic nanoparticles that can reduce precious metal content and enhance activity and stability,” Wu said.Cage the nanoparticlesHydrogen fuel cells produce clean electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen, leaving behind nothing but heat and pure water. To drive that reaction efficiently, fuel cells rely on platinum, a rare, expensive metal. Platinum is a great catalyst for energy conversion. Engineers shrink bulk platinum down to tiny nanoparticles to maximize its surface area. It works to achieve strong catalytic performance with tiny amounts, but only for a while. Under operational stress, those tiny nanoparticles dissolve, drift, and clump together, gradually degrading during fuel-cell operation.Also, heating platinum-cobalt alloys above 700°C creates a highly ordered intermetallic structure that drastically improves durability. But at those blistering temperatures, the nanoparticles aggregate.Smaller particles mean more activity. Bigger particles mean longer lifespans. Until now, scientists had to pick one.In this new work, the team decided to overcome this issue by redesigning the underlying carbon support. And designed a porous, hollow carbon spheres built with ordered, radial nanochannels. These tiny carbon cages lock the platinum-cobalt nanoparticles in place.Nanostructures perform well in testing This specialized high-surface-area architecture securely anchors dense, well-dispersed platinum-cobalt nanoparticles, allowing them to withstand the high temperatures required to form a fully ordered intermetallic phase without clumping or losing their fine dispersion.Standard methods are limited to maximum heating temperatures below 700°C and suffer from particle clumping at high heat. The new approach tolerates temperatures up to 1000°C while maintaining precise particle sizes under 5 nanometers.Furthermore, this structural stability under high heat translates directly into exceptional operational longevity. Interestingly, the nanostructures retain 85% of their output even after 150,000 cycles.The open channels also help ionomers spread evenly. That lets protons, oxygen, and water move effortlessly through the electrode during operation.“As a result, the platinum cobalt nanoparticles built into this support showed best-in-class performance and long-lasting durability,” Wu said.The rapid expansion of US data centers is driving a sharp rise in power demand, with annual electricity consumption projected to more than double from 4% of total generation in 2023 to up to 9% by 2030. To address these growing energy and cooling needs, commercializing resilient fuel cells with industrial partners offers a viable solution. It could allow facility operators to depend less on local utilities by generating electricity on-site directly from hydrogen.The team aims to collaborate with industry partners to resolve remaining catalyst challenges and accelerate the development of highly efficient, sustainable fuel cell technologies.The study was published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology on August 6.

title: Nuclear firm advances 986°F lead-cooled reactor, MOX fuel in US filing
content: Nuclear technology firm newcleo has taken its first formal step toward building a commercial fuel recycling plant in the United States. The company submitted a framework document, known as a Regulatory Engagement Plan, to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. This step allows federal inspectors and company engineers to review safety designs and technical standards long before official licensing begins.This move matches a separate review already underway for newcleo’s lead-cooled fast reactor, the LFR-AS-200. By licensing both the reactor design and the fuel factory together, the company hopes to create a complete domestic fuel loop inside North America.Most commercial power plants rely on light-water reactors. These conventional systems use water to slow down neutrons during the nuclear reaction. While this process generates electricity reliably, it leaves behind used fuel that contains unspent energy and heavy radioactive elements.In contrast, fast-spectrum reactors operate without water moderators. Because the neutrons move at higher energy levels, they can split heavy transuranic elements, including various plutonium isotopes and minor actinides. Standard thermal reactors cannot break these elements down effectively.To manufacture mixed-oxide fuelThe proposed American facility will manufacture mixed-oxide fuel, commonly called MOX. Workers blend reprocessed plutonium from old nuclear waste with stockpiles of depleted uranium. Recycling these actinides into fresh fuel changes how engineers manage long-term radioactive waste.When reactors burn transuranic elements in a fast neutron spectrum, the remaining waste loses its high radioactivity much faster. The hazard level drops to natural background levels in hundreds of years, rather than the hundreds of thousands of years required for conventional waste. At the same time, reusing existing material removes the need to mine fresh uranium or run isotopic enrichment plants for every new fuel batch.The planned MOX plant will supply fuel directly to the LFR-AS-200, a small modular reactor designed to produce 200 megawatts of electricity. Instead of high-pressure water, this reactor uses pure liquid lead as its primary coolant.Liquid lead offers strong physical safety advantages. It boils at temperatures above 1,700°C, which allows the cooling loop to operate safely at normal atmospheric pressure without heavy containment domes. Lead also does not catch fire when exposed to air or water.Inside the reactor core, steel pins packed with MOX fuel sit in tight hexagonal patterns. Liquid lead can corrode steel over time at normal operating temperatures of 530°C (about 990°F). To stop this damage, engineers apply a microscopic layer of protective alumina onto the steel cladding using laser technology. The core also uses different plutonium concentrations across its central and outer regions. Varying the fuel strength between 14.6 percent and 23.2 percent keeps the power output smooth and even across the entire reactor core.Licensing work already underwayThe American filing expands on licensing work already underway in Europe. French safety authorities recently accepted the initial safety options dossier for a sister MOX facility planned in France.Because plutonium emits alpha radiation, human workers cannot touch the material directly. Equipment must operate inside sealed gloveboxes using automated tools and robotics.To test these systems, newcleo built a non-radioactive testing center in Chusclan, France, named FASTER. Engineers there use full-scale mechanical mock-ups, robotic arms, and virtual control systems. By testing pellet presses, pin welders, and automated inspection tools without live radiation, the team fixes mechanical issues before the equipment enters commercial service.

title: Nuclear firms explore recycled materials to fuel next-gen reactors
content: Three nuclear companies are exploring a new way to turn recycled nuclear materials into fuel for next-generation reactors, potentially linking fuel recycling, manufacturing and advanced reactor technology into a single supply chain.Curio, NuScale Power and Framatome have signed a memorandum of understanding to evaluate how materials recovered through Curio’s NuCycle recycling technology could be used in future nuclear fuel and other products. Curio develops nuclear fuel recycling technology, NuScale makes small modular reactors, and Framatome supplies nuclear fuel and reactor systems. The work will focus on technical feasibility, fuel development, manufacturing, and potential commercialization.The companies will examine both “source-to-product” and “source-to-fuel” pathways, essentially looking at how recovered materials could move from used nuclear fuel into new applications. They will also assess supply-chain requirements and how their technologies could work together.The agreement comes as the nuclear industry faces growing demand for new reactors while also trying to build more resilient domestic fuel supplies. The companies say an integrated fuel cycle could help support advanced reactors in the US and nuclear energy projects in international markets.Recycling meets reactor demandCurio brings the fuel-recycling side of the partnership. Its NuCycle technology is designed to process used nuclear fuel and recover materials for potential reuse. The company says the technology could reduce residual waste volumes by up to 97% while recovering strategic nuclear materials.NuScale brings its small modular reactor technology to the collaboration. Its NuScale Power Module is a pressurized water reactor designed to generate 77 megawatts of electricity per module, with multiple modules able to be combined into larger plants.Framatome adds expertise in nuclear fuel manufacturing and reactor services. The company designs and supplies nuclear fuel and other systems used across the global nuclear fleet.“America’s ability to lead the next era of nuclear energy will depend on more than building reactors—it will require building the fuel cycle infrastructure needed to support them,” said Ed McGinnis, CEO of Curio.The companies will conduct technical assessments, feasibility studies, supply-chain analyses and interface evaluations under the MOU. These studies are intended to identify areas where the three companies could pursue more detailed development agreements or commercial partnerships.Building fuel for reactorsThe partnership is not yet a commercial fuel-production deal. Instead, it establishes a framework for determining whether recovered nuclear materials can be turned into usable fuel and products at scale.For advanced reactors, having a dependable fuel supply can be as important as developing the reactor itself. The partners will therefore examine requirements spanning material recovery, fuel development, qualification and fabrication before potential commercial deployment.“Advancing the next generation of nuclear energy demands bold innovation and strong alignment across the entire fuel cycle,” said Tony Robinson, Framatome Inc. President and CEO. “At Framatome, we are committed to working with partners who share that vision and support efforts to strengthen America’s nuclear infrastructure.“NuScale also sees the fuel cycle as a key part of deploying SMRs. “With the most near-term deployable SMR technology, NuScale has long recognized that the nuclear industry requires a strong, reliable, sustainable frontend and backend fuel supply to meet increasing demand,” said John Hopkins, President and CEO of NuScale Power.The companies say the collaboration could eventually lead to new agreements covering technology development, fuel qualification, supply-chain development and commercial deployment. For now, the goal is to determine whether recycled nuclear materials can become part of a more integrated fuel system for the next generation of reactors.

title: Passenger pods jump from roads to rails without riders stepping out
content: A new modular mobility concept could allow passengers and cargo to move between roads, railways, and even cable cars without ever leaving the same transport capsule.The concept is part of the EU-funded Pods4Rail initiative. It was developed by the German Aerospace Center (DLR), along with other research and industry partners, and coordinated by Siemens Mobility. The project involved 15 participants from seven European countries. The system uses standardized passenger and freight capsules, called pods. These can automatically transfer between specialized carrier units designed for different modes of transport. Each carrier unit provides the parts necessary for its particular transport mode, such as the chassis, propulsion system, power supply, and other technical equipment. “The aim of Pods4Rail is to provide seamless end-to-end mobility across different modes of transport,” Manuel Osebek, a DLR researcher who led the project, said. “Passengers and freight remain in the same capsule throughout a journey, being transferred to another carrier unit as required.”Rethinking transportationDLR described the approach as supermodality. Under the concept, the rail would serve as the backbone of the proposed transportation network. For example, a passenger pod could start its journey attached to a road carrier in a rural area.However after reaching a transport hub, the entire capsule could be automatically transferred onto a rail carrier. Multiple pods could then travel together by rail for the longer part of the journey before separating and returning to road-based carriers closer to their destinations.The pods for the transport of people and goods can be combined with different carrier units.Credit: Pods4Rail project group / moodleyFor the study, we did not just look at the vehicles required for such a concept,” Osebek stressed. “Other key aspects included how pods and carrier units could be connected to one another, as well as issues relating to automation.”The researchers also investigated whether cable cars could become another part of the network. This would potentially allow the same pods to move across three different modes of transportation. The approach could move more journeys onto energy-efficient railways while still offering the flexibility of road travel.”“Analyses of the necessary infrastructure and ideas for digital operating concepts rounded off the work,” Osebek said in a press release. The EU project benefited from the diverse expertise of its participants.More than travelThe team also investigated safety standards and approval requirements for both road and rail transportation. They identified more than 20 potential applications and developed eight business scenarios for the technology.DLR noted that the technology’s potential uses range from on-demand passenger services on underused railway branch lines to parcel and express deliveries. The researchers even envision specialized pods serving as mobile medical facilities.With seamless transfers between multiple modes of transport, Pods4Rail aims to open up new possibilities in the mobility sector.Credit: Pods4Rail project group / moodleyThe concept got nearly USD 3.5 million (EUR three million) in funding through the Europe’s Rail Joint Undertaking (ERJU) and Horizon Europe program. Future work will also need to address regulatory approval, economic viability, and integration with existing transportation infrastructure.At the same time, a DLR-led follow-up project called PREFER, short for Pods and Regional Flexible Efficient Rolling Stock, is expected to begin later this year and take the modular transportation concept into its next stage of development.

title: The supersonic comeback is closer than it has been in decades
content:
The Concorde last flew in 2003, bringing to an end the first era of supersonic commercial flight.
Fast forward 23 years and we are now on the verge of a new era of supersonic aviation. It is made possible by over two decades of technological advances, allowing for more efficient, quieter supersonic aircraft.
The company leading the charge towards this new period of commercial travel is Boom Supersonic. Since it was founded in 2014, the company has touted a spiritual successor to the Concorde.

title: US Air Force taps Eaton to build smarter defenses for power grid
content: Eaton, a U.S. power management company, has landed a $7 million contract from the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) to develop quantum computing tools aimed at protecting the nation’s electric grid from increasing cyber and physical threats.The company announced the two-year project on Thursday. Eaton will team up with Infleqtion and Pennsylvania State University to develop new quantum-powered ways to detect and respond to several grid failures at once.The research will use quantum computing, machine learning, and advanced visualization to help power operators spot vulnerabilities and handle disruptions. The goal is to make the grid more resilient as utilities deal with more severe weather, wildfires, cyberattacks, and other risks.Tackling a growing grid security challengeA key part of the project is solving what engineers call the contingency problem. This means analyzing countless possible operating conditions to find weak spots in the power grid before anything goes wrong.Current reliability standards set by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) require transmission systems to keep working after two failures in a row, a standard called N-2 planning. Eaton’s research aims to go further by looking at several failures happening at once, so operators can better understand all possible risks.The company plans to use its power management experience along with quantum computing’s strength in handling complex calculations. By using a mix of quantum and classical computing, the company hopes to find grid vulnerabilities faster and more accurately, and suggest better responses.“We’re facing unprecedented risks to electric reliability and security from extreme weather, wildfires, physical and cyber threats, and need tools that consider many failures at once,” stressed Sid Suryanarayanan, senior chief engineer, strategic partnerships and innovation at Eaton. “This AFRL-funded project pairs Eaton’s grid expertise with quantum and machine learning methods to bring faster awareness and more actionable control to critical energy systems.”Quantum and machine learning join forcesThe project brings together experts from several organizations. Infleqtion will supply specialized quantum hardware, and researchers at Pennsylvania State University will contribute advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence skills.The team will work together to create new quantum algorithms, improve circuits for hybrid quantum-classical computing, and test them on different quantum hardware. They will also try to reduce computational errors, which is one of the main technical challenges for today’s quantum computers.The goal is to create practical tools that utilities can eventually use to improve infrastructure planning, support daily grid operations, and strengthen emergency response during major disruptions.Demonstration planned after two-year projectAs part of the AFRL-funded effort, the research team will produce a proof-of-concept demonstration showing how existing quantum hardware, combined with newly developed algorithms and machine learning techniques, can address real-world electric grid challenges.The demonstration is expected to highlight how quantum-enabled technologies could help operators visualize complex grid conditions, evaluate multiple threat scenarios, and make faster operational decisions during emergencies.“At Eaton, we’re delivering next-generation solutions for intelligent power management that benefit critical infrastructure through our world-class engineering capabilities and our comprehensive approach to research and development,” said Dr. Christopher A. Herbst, vice president, strategic partnerships and innovation at Eaton. “This research will enhance infrastructure planning, daily operations and emergency preparedness, bringing unprecedented awareness, anticipation and response to strengthen infrastructure.”

title: US tests Ghost Bat's ability to operate without permanent base
content: Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat completed multiple operational sorties during Valiant Shield 2026, testing how the uncrewed aircraft could deploy and fly from an austere Pacific location.From June 21 to July 1, the U.S. Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit operated the aircraft at Rota in the Northern Mariana Islands, with support from the 21st Air Expeditionary Wing. The 11-day deployment evaluated the personnel, infrastructure and resources required to sustain future Collaborative Combat Aircraft away from established bases.Testing combat aircraft under realistic conditionsThe exercise moved the MQ-28 beyond a controlled test setting and placed it inside a large-force event under operationally relevant conditions. Teams assessed the power, fuel, communications and security needed to keep the aircraft functioning remotely.“The EOU conducts rapid experimentation with CCA prototypes to provide direct warfighter feedback to CCA and mission-autonomy vendors,” said U.S. Air Force Maj. Daniel Pesich, EOU combat aircraft detachment officer in charge. “The unit is uniquely designed to take emerging technologies like the CCA and place them into operationally relevant environments much earlier than traditional acquisition programs,” he added.The EOU studied both the deployment and sustainment requirements associated with Collaborative Combat Aircraft. According to the Air Force, lessons from activities that worked, as well as those that did not, will help shape how CCA are developed and employed.“This is the first of many large force exercises the EOU will participate in with the CCA. We will build from this event with the intent of quickly integrating with the force more each time,” said Pesich.Support network enables MQ-28 sortiesThe 21st Air Expeditionary Wing established the support network required for the flights. Its personnel handled power production, communications and force protection, creating the foundation upon which the aircraft and its operators depended.“The ability of our team to work in the background is the foundation necessary for MQ-28 operations,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Nathaniel White, 21st CABS commander. “Without power the ground control unit wouldn’t be functional, without fuel the power wouldn’t be supplied, and without communications we wouldn’t be able to provide the MQ-28 operators the necessary capabilities to plan,” he continued. The wing supported decentralized activity across four islands in the Guam cluster. Its responsibilities included managing airfields, refueling and defueling aircraft, moving logistics and protecting assets.Lessons for future US collaborative aircraftThe sorties showed how the Ghost Bat could be incorporated into expeditionary operations under the Air Force’s Agile Combat Employment concept. That approach is designed to distribute forces and reduce reliance on a small number of permanent operating locations.The deployment also gave warfighters an opportunity to provide direct feedback to mission-autonomy developers. Such observations could influence the technologies, support systems and operational concepts adopted by future U.S. collaborative aircraft programs.For the EOU, Valiant Shield marked an early step rather than a final demonstration. Large-force exercises are expected to increase the MQ-28’s integration with other elements of the force while exposing the aircraft to more demanding scenarios.

title: World's first self-driving robot from Hyundai works aboard moving ship
content: Hyundai Motor Group (HMG) has successfully demonstrated what they describe as the world’s first autonomous self-driving robot operating aboard a moving ship, marking a step toward safer maritime inspections. The MobED (Mobile Eccentric Droid) mobile robot completed trials aboard the multipurpose vessel HYUNDAI DUBAI in South Korea, proving it could navigate despite constant vibration, vessel motion, and uneven surfaces. The technology could eventually inspect enclosed cargo holds and other hazardous spaces that may be too dangerous or toxic for seafarers to enter.In December 2025, Hyundai first unveiled its autonomous MobED robot, a compact four-wheeled platform designed for industrial and everyday applications, ahead of future mass production.Autonomous robot sailsMobED was tested aboard the multipurpose vessel HYUNDAI DUBAI during a joint demonstration involving Korean Register (KR), HMM, HMM Ocean Service and Goseong Engineering in Changwon, South Korea.The trial evaluated whether an autonomous robot originally designed for land-based environments could operate reliably aboard a moving ship, where constant vibration, vessel motion and uneven surfaces present unique navigation challenges. The demonstration forms part of efforts to advance smart ship technologies by deploying robots for cargo hold inspections, condition monitoring and material transport in areas that may be hazardous or difficult for crew members to access.During the tests, MobED successfully carried out a range of autonomous navigation tasks inside the vessel’s cargo spaces, including straight and curved driving, low- and high-speed movement, route learning and fully autonomous operation. Its independently controlled wheel system enabled the robot to maintain stability while traversing uneven decks, inclines and thresholds commonly found aboard ships.The platform can also be fitted with inspection equipment, cameras and delivery modules, allowing it to perform different onboard tasks. In narrow passageways, the robot completed route-learning and low-speed navigation, although operators switched it to remote-control mode because of the confined space. The project partners said the successful demonstration showed autonomous robots can work effectively inside large cargo areas without requiring modifications to existing ship infrastructure.Multi-purpose mobility robotMobED is a compact four-wheeled autonomous robot developed by HMG’s Robotics Lab to navigate environments that are difficult for conventional robots. Built on the company’s proprietary Drive and Lift (DnL) technology, the platform features independently controlled wheels that automatically adjust to maintain a level surface while traveling over steep ramps, curbs, rocky terrain and uneven ground. This stability allows it to safely transport fragile equipment, cameras and other sensitive payloads across challenging environments.The robot is available in two versions: MobED Basic and MobED Pro, each designed for different applications. The Pro model combines LiDAR and camera sensors with AI-powered navigation, enabling it to move autonomously through crowded environments. It also includes a “follow-me” mode that allows it to accompany users while carrying equipment or supplies. The Basic model, meanwhile, is remotely operated and intended for researchers and developers building customized robotic applications.Designed for both industrial and consumer use, MobED can support a variety of attachments, including inspection tools, delivery boxes, cameras, digital displays and advertising screens. Hyundai says the platform can be used for last-mile logistics, facility inspections, broadcasting support, digital guidance services and mobile advertising. The Basic model can carry payloads of up to 47 kilograms (103 pounds). In comparison, the Pro version supports up to 57 kilograms (125 pounds) and reaches speeds of 10 km/h, making it suitable for a wide range of commercial and service applications.

title: GCL Optoelectronics raises over US$14 million in D1 financing round, certifies 30.23% efficiency for large-area perovskite tandem module
content:
GCL Optoelectronics raises over US$14 million in D1 financing round, certifies 30.23% efficiency for large-area perovskite tandem module
GCL Optoelectronic Material
(Kunshan GCL Optoelectronic Materials), a subsidiary of GCL Group, has completed a D1 financing round exceeding 100 million yuan (over US$14 million), led by Jinxin Capital, with Sequoia China, Xiang'an Venture Capital and Suzhou Asset Management participating. The company says the funds will primarily support the commercial delivery of its ground-mounted photovoltaic power stations and the verification of space photovoltaic applications.
The D1 round follows
a Series C2 round completed in July 2025
that raised nearly 200 million yuan. Since its first angel round in May 2020, GCL Optoelectronics has attracted strategic investments exceeding one billion yuan from companies and institutions including CATL, TCL Group, Tencent, Temasek and Sequoia Capital.
GCL Optoelectronics has focused on perovskite technology since 2013 and describes itself as one of the world's earliest companies to pursue industrialization of perovskite modules, crediting itself with several industry firsts: the industry's first 100MW-level perovskite R&D line, the industry's first 2-square-meter perovskite module, and the industry's first high-throughput R&D equipment. On the ground-application side, the company's 2-square-meter perovskite tandem module has reached a certified efficiency of 27% and obtained what the company describes as the industry's first tandem module IEC dual-standard certification. Its GW-level Phase I production line, with a total module area of 2.78 square meters across all specifications, has a certification efficiency of 26.8% and is being used to advance product verification and market entry for ground-mounted power plants, industrial and commercial distributed PV, and building-integrated PV; the company says it has signed multiple MW-level module orders so far this year.
The company also reports two newly certified efficiency records. Certified by the National Institute of Metrology of China, a 2042 cm² perovskite-crystalline silicon tandem module reached 30.23% efficiency, which GCL Optoelectronics describes as officially crossing the 30% efficiency threshold for a module of this size. Separately, certified by TÜV SÜD, a 900 cm² flexible single-junction module reached 21.79% efficiency and a 625 cm² flexible tandem module reached 27.11% - which the company says breaks the world record for flexible perovskite module efficiency.
Dr. Fan Bin, Chairman of GCL Optoelectronics, said: "Over the past sixteen years, our team has personally experienced and witnessed multiple cycles of evolution in the photovoltaic industry and perovskite technology. Currently, perovskite is entering a critical window of opportunity for large-scale application. In particular, in this round of financing, we have won the trust and support of new and old shareholders such as Jinxin Capital, Sequoia China, Xiang'an Venture Capital, and Suzhou Asset Management, which has further strengthened our strategic commitment to long-term development in the perovskite industrialization." He added: "Looking ahead, the company will continue to focus on the core perovskite sector, actively seize the opportunities brought by new scenarios such as space photovoltaics, and promote perovskite technology to a wider range of applications."

title: Novel doping strategy boosts efficiency and stability of all-inorganic solar cells
content:
Novel doping strategy boosts efficiency and stability of all-inorganic solar cells
Researchers from Guangdong University of Technology have developed a zinc-ion (Zn
) modification strategy that improves both the efficiency and the stability of all-inorganic CsPbBr
perovskite solar cells.
All-inorganic CsPbBr
perovskites are known for their excellent environmental stability compared with hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites, since they avoid the organic cations (such as MA
) that are prone to degrading under heat, moisture, oxygen and light. That stability comes at a cost, however: CsPbBr
's wide bandgap (about 2.3 eV) limits light harvesting, and its films typically suffer from low crystallinity and high defect density, which drive charge recombination and hold back power conversion efficiency (PCE).
The team's Zn
modification strategy is designed to address the film-quality side of that trade-off. Introducing Zn
optimizes the crystallization of the CsPbBr
film, producing a denser, pinhole-free morphology with larger grain size and improved crystallinity. That microstructural improvement enhances light absorption and suppresses non-radiative recombination losses. The 0.5% Zn
-modified device achieved a champion PCE of 8.54%, a 21% improvement over the 7.07% efficiency of the unmodified control device. The unencapsulated modified device also retained over 91.6% of its initial efficiency after 720 hours (30 days) of storage at 80°C and 80% relative humidity.
The researchers note that metal-ion doping has become a common strategy for improving CsPbBr
PSCs, citing prior work using dopants such as Sm
(10.14% PCE), Sr
(9.63% PCE) and Sn
(efficiency raised from 6.85% to 8.63%). They point to zinc's low cost, natural abundance, low toxicity and stable +2 oxidation state as reasons for exploring it as a modifier, alongside evidence from other studies that moderate Zn
doping improves crystallinity and grain size in perovskite films.
